member.name: T:OpenIGI.Game.Igi1.Physics.RagdollBody
member.content: The contacts: the ground surveyed once a tick, the bones projected out of it and out of each other, and the friction and restitution read back from the contact velocities.
member.summary: A corpse being simulated: one rigid body per bone, stepped on the game's own tick.

remarks.para: This is presentation, not simulation. The body it belongs to keeps its retail death exactly — the same tick, the same authoritative position, the same consequences for the AI around it. What a ragdoll changes is the pose that is drawn, and nothing reads back out of it into the game.

Extended position-based dynamics: each tick is divided into substeps, each substep integrates forwards and then projects every constraint once, and the velocities are read back out of how far things actually moved. See for the mathematics and for the reference.

It is stepped on the 30 Hz tick rather than per frame, so it lands on the same grid as everything else the presentation interpolates between; r_smooth and the temporal resolve then get their between-tick blend for free from the mesh's own previous-pose stream.

member.content: The joints: the friction that bleeds a bone's spin relative to its parent, and the attachment and swing-limit projections that hold each bone to its parent.

member.name: M:OpenIGI.Game.Igi1.Physics.RagdollBody.Survey(OpenIGI.Game.Physics.RagdollWorld)
member.summary: Finds the ground under every probe, once for the whole tick.

remarks.para: The one thing that decides whether ragdolls are affordable. Asking the world where the floor is costs a ray cast against every placed collision mesh plus a terrain lookup — easily the most expensive call in the solver, and thousands of times more expensive than the arithmetic around it. Doing it inside the projection meant 1349 of them per corpse per tick: three probes a bone, sixteen substeps, two passes. Ten corpses were costing more than the frame.

It is also unnecessary. A bone moves a few units in a substep, so the surface under it does not change within a tick even though its distance to that surface does — and only the distance is wanted per projection. So the plane is found once and the penetration recomputed against it every time, which is the same split the XPBD paper makes between collecting collision pairs once a frame and recomputing each contact every substep.
What it costs is a tick of lag on the surface itself: a bone that slides over a step edge uses the old floor until the next tick. At thirty ticks a second, on a corpse, that is not observable.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Game.Igi1.Physics.RagdollBody.Gravity
member.summary: How fast a corpse falls, in engine units per tick squared.

remarks.para: Not the same gravity the player falls at, and the difference is not invented. The original pulls a walking human down at — 18.6 m/s², very nearly twice life — because a platformer's jump reads better heavy and snappy. A corpse is not jumping; it is an object, and at that rate it drops like a stone and the fall reads as sped-up film.

So a ragdoll uses the other gravity the original already carries: , which is exactly 9.8 m/s² and is what the engine itself uses for the one case where a human is falling rather than moving. No number is invented here — both are the game's own, and this picks the one that describes a body.

Scaling below it is a different kind of decision and is kept separate. Real gravity reads fast on a corpse — the camera is close, the fall is short, and there is no anticipation to sell it — so games routinely drop a ragdoll under one g for legibility. That is a look, not a measurement, so it lives in g_ragdoll_gravity where it can be seen and turned rather than baked into a constant that claims to be physics.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Game.Igi1.Physics.RagdollBody.LinearDamping
member.summary: What fraction of a body's speed survives one tick.
member.remarks: Air drag, and small: what actually stops a corpse is the ground it is lying on.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Game.Igi1.Physics.RagdollBody.AngularDamping
member.summary: What fraction of a body's spin survives one tick.
member.remarks: The single most important number for whether a ragdoll reads as a body or as a rag. Limbs keep spinning long after the torso has stopped moving, and nothing else in the solver takes that energy out — the joints only say where a limb may be, not how fast it may get there.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Game.Igi1.Physics.RagdollBody.JointDamping
member.summary: How strongly a joint resists its two bones turning relative to one another.
member.remarks: Joint friction, and it is what makes a corpse limp rather than loose. Distinct from , which slows a limb against the world: this slows it against the limb it hangs off, so a whole body can tumble freely while its elbows stay quiet.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Game.Igi1.Physics.RagdollBody.Restitution
member.summary: How much of a bone's speed into a surface comes back out of it.
member.remarks: Nothing. A body is not a ball, and restitution on a ragdoll only ever makes it twitch.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Game.Igi1.Physics.RagdollBody.Friction
member.summary: How much of a bone's speed along a surface survives a contact.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Game.Igi1.Physics.RagdollBody.TorsionalFriction
member.summary: How much of a bone's spin is rubbed off each substep it is touching something.

remarks.para: Torsional friction, and without it a corpse spins on the ground for a very long time. Sliding friction acts on how fast a contact point is travelling, which says nothing about a body turning about the very axis it is resting on: the contact is stationary, the friction sees nothing to oppose, and only the slow global air damping is left to stop it. A real contact patch resists twisting as well as sliding, and this is that.

Applied to bones that are actually touching, so a body in mid-air still tumbles freely. At eight substeps a bone in contact loses about three quarters of its spin a tick, which reads as a body that comes to rest rather than one that winds down.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Game.Igi1.Physics.RagdollBody.PenetrationSlop
member.summary: How far a bone may sink into a surface before it is pushed out, in engine units.
member.remarks: Two centimetres, and it is a deadband rather than a target. Correcting penetration to exactly zero makes a resting body flicker between touching and not touching, which reads as a corpse humming against the floor.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Game.Igi1.Physics.RagdollBody.MaximumDepenetrationSpeed
member.summary: The fastest a bone may be pushed out of geometry, in engine units per tick.

remarks.para: The single most important number in the contact solve, and leaving it out is what makes a ragdoll dance. Velocities here are not stored, they are read back out of how far things moved — so a positional correction of d over a substep of h is a velocity of d/h. Pushing a bone out of eight centimetres of floor in one sixteenth of a tick therefore hands it sixteen times that in upward speed, and the corpse launches, cartwheels and never settles.

A quarter of a metre a tick, about 7 m/s. Deep penetration is walked out over several substeps instead of being fired out in one. From Macklin et al., Small Steps in Physics Simulation, section 4.3, where it is the fix for exactly this.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Game.Igi1.Physics.RagdollBody.RestThresholdInUnits
member.summary: How far a body may drift in a tick and still count as having stopped, in engine units.
member.remarks: Five millimetres a tick, averaged over the bones. It is not zero and cannot be: a settled body is still pulled into the floor by gravity and pushed back out by the contact every substep, and what is left over after those cancel is a hum far below anything visible.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Game.Igi1.Physics.RagdollBody.SettleSpeedInUnits
member.summary: How fast a body may still be moving and count as trying to settle.
member.remarks: The settling help must not fight the shot. A guard is standing on the floor when he is killed, so he is already in contact at the instant the round throws him — and a ramp that keys purely off contact starts scrubbing the throw away immediately, which is why bodies dropped flat where they stood instead of being knocked back. A body only counts as settling once it is actually slow; while it is still travelling it is left alone.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Game.Igi1.Physics.RagdollBody.RestTicks
member.summary: How many consecutive still ticks latch a body at rest.
member.remarks: Twelve — four tenths of a second. It is a confirmation that the body has stopped, not a waiting period: a full second of stillness before the latch is a full second of a corpse that has already finished still being simulated.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Game.Igi1.Physics.RagdollBody.SettleRampTicks
member.summary: Over how many ticks ON THE GROUND the settling help reaches full strength.

remarks.para: Counted from first contact, not from death, and that is the whole point. Timing it from the moment of death means a body that is still falling gets helped to stop — and, worse, a body that has landed gets no help at all until the clock says so, which is exactly the couple of seconds of twitching on the ground this exists to remove.

It is also the physically honest place for it. A body tumbling through the air really does keep its energy; a body lying on the ground really is losing it to whatever it is lying on, far faster than the point friction at a handful of contacts can account for.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Game.Igi1.Physics.RagdollBody.MaximumActiveTicks
member.summary: After how many ticks a body is put to rest whatever it is doing.

remarks.para: Ten seconds. A guarantee rather than a tuning value. A constraint solver of this shape has no proof that it converges — the paper it is built from says as much about piles, and a corpse lying on the ground with its own joints and a dozen contacts fighting each other is a pile. In practice a body settles in about three seconds; in the cases that do not, the failure a player sees is a corpse twitching or slowly turning on the spot for the rest of the mission, and it goes on costing solver time the whole while.
Ten seconds after it died, it stops. Nothing that has not settled by then was going to.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Game.Igi1.Physics.RagdollBody.SettleDamping
member.summary: How much of a body's spin the settling ramp takes away at full strength.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Game.Igi1.Physics.RagdollBody.WallProbes
member.summary: How many ways a bone looks for a wall each tick.

remarks.para: Two, and which two matters more than how many. One along the way the bone is travelling, which is what catches a body being thrown into a wall, and one straight out from the body's own centre, which is what catches a body already resting against one. Casting along the axes instead would need four and still miss a diagonal.
Like the ground, they are collected once a tick and resolved every substep — the surface beside a bone does not move within a tick even though the bone's distance to it does.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Game.Igi1.Physics.RagdollBody.SolverPasses
member.summary: How many times each substep projects the contacts and then the joints.
member.remarks: Two. Substepping is the real convergence knob and passes are the expensive one, so this stays small — but it cannot be one, because the contacts and the joints each undo a little of what the other did and a single pass leaves whichever ran first entirely unrepaired.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Game.Igi1.Physics.RagdollBody.JointStiffness
member.summary: How much of a joint's excursion past what it allows is taken out each substep.
member.remarks: Two fifths. See for what this holds and why it is a spring rather than a stop. It is paired with the substep count — the spring acts once per pass, so halving the substeps halves how much it removes per tick — and this is the value at which a joint driven to its limit settles back onto it rather than resting outside it.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Game.Igi1.Physics.RagdollBody.JointIterations
member.summary: How many times each pass projects the joint list.
member.remarks: One. already walks the joint list twice a substep, and a third and fourth walk measurably cost more than they straighten — the substep count is where convergence actually comes from.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Game.Igi1.Physics.RagdollBody.RunawayDistanceInUnits
member.summary: How far from its origin a body may get before it is abandoned, in engine units.
member.remarks: A backstop, not a limit. A corpse has no business travelling a hundred metres from where it died, so a body that has is a body whose solver has gone wrong — and the failure a player sees is that the corpse vanishes, because it is drawn correctly, half a mile away. Catching it here means the worst case is falling back to the retail death animation rather than losing the body altogether.

member.name: P:OpenIGI.Game.Igi1.Physics.RagdollBody.Rig
member.summary: Gets the rig this body wears.

member.name: P:OpenIGI.Game.Igi1.Physics.RagdollBody.Origin
member.summary: Gets the frozen world position the drawn pose is expressed relative to, in engine units.
member.remarks: Fixed when the body is seeded and never moved. The pose is built relative to it with no rotation applied, so the renderer draws the corpse by placing it here with an identity orientation — the world turn is carried inside the root bone's own rotation.

member.name: P:OpenIGI.Game.Igi1.Physics.RagdollBody.IsAtRest
member.summary: Gets whether the body has stopped moving and no longer needs stepping.

member.name: P:OpenIGI.Game.Igi1.Physics.RagdollBody.IsValid
member.summary: Gets whether the simulation is still producing sensible results.
member.remarks: Once this goes false the body must be dropped and the retail death animation drawn instead. It is a backstop against the failure mode a player actually reports, which is not "the physics look wrong" but "the body vanished" — a corpse drawn perfectly well a mile outside the level, or at coordinates that are not numbers at all, is invisible either way.

member.name: P:OpenIGI.Game.Igi1.Physics.RagdollBody.BoneCount
member.summary: Gets how many bones the drawn skeleton has.
member.remarks: The skeleton's own count, which is not the number of bodies being simulated — anything the corpse is carrying is a body too, and sits past the end of this.

member.name: P:OpenIGI.Game.Igi1.Physics.RagdollBody.HasAttachment
member.summary: Gets whether this corpse is carrying something that is being simulated with it.

member.name: P:OpenIGI.Game.Igi1.Physics.RagdollBody.AttachmentPosition
member.summary: Gets where the carried body's own origin sits, relative to .
member.remarks: Its origin rather than its centre of mass, because that is the point a weapon's mesh is modelled about and so the point it has to be drawn at.

member.name: P:OpenIGI.Game.Igi1.Physics.RagdollBody.AttachmentRotation
member.summary: Gets which way the carried body is facing.

member.remarks: What a camera should frame, and it needs no bone to be named to find it — which matters, because the retail rigs' bone roles have not been measured and "the chest" would be a guess.

member.name: M:OpenIGI.Game.Igi1.Physics.RagdollBody.Seed(OpenIGI.Game.Igi1.Physics.RagdollSkeleton,OpenIGI.Formats.Animation.BonePose,OpenIGI.Core.Numerics.Vector3d,OpenIGI.Core.Numerics.Matrix3f,System.Nullable{OpenIGI.Game.Igi1.Physics.RagdollBone},System.Int32)
member.summary: Starts a ragdoll from the pose a body was drawn in when it died.
member.param: The prepared rig.
The last animated pose, in the body's own model space — what SoldierView.UnrotatedPose() yields.
Where that model space sits in the world, in engine units.
The body's heading, applied to the pose to reach world space.
Something the body is carrying — a weapon — as a rigid body of its own, or for empty hands. It is placed at 's transform and jointed to it.
Which bone holds the attachment.
member.returns: The seeded body, at rest and with no velocity.

member.summary: Pushes one bone.

member.remarks: The generalized inverse mass of each body includes the (r × n)ᵀ I⁻¹ (r × n) term, which is what makes a push at the end of a limb rotate it rather than slide it. A body index of −1 is the world: infinitely heavy, and it takes none of the correction.

member.name: M:OpenIGI.Game.Igi1.Physics.RagdollBody.Turn(System.Int32,OpenIGI.Core.Numerics.Vector3d)
member.summary: Turns a bone, keeping its cached rotation matrix in step with its quaternion.
member.remarks: The matrix is cached because rebuilding it was the solver's largest single cost. Every vector this thing rotates — three contact probes a bone, two anchors a joint, two axes a self-collision pair, every substep, every pass — went through a quaternion-to-matrix conversion first, and there are far more rotations than there are orientation changes. Keeping the matrix beside the quaternion turns each of those into a plain multiply.

member.name: M:OpenIGI.Game.Igi1.Physics.RagdollBody.SolveDeviation(OpenIGI.Game.Igi1.Physics.RagdollJoint)
member.summary: Eases a bone back toward its parent whenever it has turned further from it than the joint allows — in any direction at all, roll included.

remarks.para: One constraint on the whole relative rotation, rather than a swing limit and a twist limit solved separately, and that is a correction rather than a simplification. Splitting a rotation into a swing and a twist needs an axis to split about, and on a joint that is already heavily swung — every joint of a corpse on the ground — the split moves part of the swing into the twist and part of the twist into the swing. Two constraints then each measure a quantity the other is changing, and neither converges: measured one way a joint would read 45°, measured the other 83°, on the same body at the same instant. The total angle between two orientations needs no axis and has no such ambiguity.

It is also what fixes the limbs going thin. Nothing else in the solver constrains a bone's roll about its own length — the attachment says where a joint is and nothing about which way the bone is turned around it — so bones rolled freely, and a skinned mesh whose bones roll relative to their neighbours pinches: the vertices wind up like a sweet wrapper and the limb narrows to a point. That reads as a broken model rather than as broken physics, which is exactly how it looked.

A soft spring rather than a hard stop, deliberately. A limit is a one-sided inequality that does nothing until it snaps, and snapping is what made the hard version shake a landed body to pieces. Taking a fixed fraction of the excess every substep acts continuously, acts hardest where the violation is worst, and cannot snap.

member.name: M:OpenIGI.Game.Igi1.Physics.RagdollBody.ApplyAngular(System.Int32,System.Int32,OpenIGI.Core.Numerics.Vector3f,System.Double,System.Boolean)
member.summary: The XPBD angular projection: turn two bodies so a rotation violation is closed.
member.remarks: A joint limit is applied as a repair, and that is what makes a corpse settle. The reasoning is the contacts' exactly: the velocities here are measured from how far things turned, so a limb shoved back inside its cone reads afterwards as a limb that was spinning that fast. On the ground the contacts push bones past their limits every substep, the limits push back, and each push-back is handed to the body as angular speed it never had — a corpse that lands and then twitches, rolls and dances, which is precisely what this looked like before the correction was excluded from the velocity.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Game.Igi1.Physics.RagdollImpulse
member.summary: What a round does to a body it kills: how hard, in which direction, and where it lands.

remarks.para: Three of the four things here are genuinely physical and come out of the shot itself — the direction is the round's own line, the point of application is the bone it went through, and the relative magnitudes between weapons are their real momenta. That is what makes a shotgun at close range throw a body and a pistol round merely drop it, without any of it being an authored table of falls.

The fourth is not physical and must not pretend to be. A 7.62 round carries about 6.8 N·s. Given to an 80 kg body that is 0.085 m/s — a barely perceptible nudge, and the reason a real person shot dead crumples rather than flies. Bodies thrown backwards by gunfire is cinema. is therefore a deliberate, authored exaggeration, recorded here as the divergence it is: it buys the reaction the shot visibly earned, at the cost of being wrong by a factor of thirty. Everything else scales off it, so the whole feel of the feature is one number, and g_ragdoll_force is that number in the player's hands.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Game.Igi1.Physics.RagdollImpulse.BodyShare
member.summary: How much of the momentum moves the whole body rather than the part that was hit.

remarks.para: Seven tenths. A round genuinely does two things to a body — it moves all of it, and it snaps the bit it went through — and the split matters because the two behave completely differently under the rig's masses. The body-wide share is applied as a velocity, so every particle gets the same one and the corpse travels as a piece; the local share is applied as a momentum, so a light limb takes far more of it than the trunk does.

Giving the whole thing to the local term is what makes a ragdoll look like a rag: a rifle round carrying enough momentum to visibly throw eighty kilograms will throw a two-kilogram forearm at a speed nothing about the shot justifies.

member.name: M:OpenIGI.Game.Igi1.Physics.RagdollImpulse.NewtonSecondsOf(OpenIGI.Game.Weapons.WeaponCategory)

member.returns: The momentum.
member.remarks: Ordinary exterior ballistics for the classes of weapon this game ships, not values read from the game's own data — the original has no such quantity, because nothing in it is ever pushed by a round. A 9 mm side-arm is about 2.9, a rifle round about 6.8, a shotgun's whole charge about 12.8, and a grenade at the body an order more than any of them.

remarks.para: The direction is the round's, unchanged and un-flattened: a shot from above drives a body down into the floor and a shot from below lifts it, which is the whole difference between this and a canned fall that only ever knows front from back.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Game.Igi1.Physics.RagdollLimits
member.summary: The range each joint of a rig actually moves through, measured from the animations the game ships for it.

remarks.para: This is what makes a corpse fold like a body rather than like a rag, and none of it is invented. A ragdoll needs to know that a knee bends one way and a shoulder rotates freely, and the usual way to supply that is a hand-written table naming bones by index — which for these rigs would be a guess, because their joint roles have never been read.

They do not need to be. The animators already answered the question: every clip the game ships is a demonstration of how far each joint is meant to move, so sweeping the rotation tracks and taking the extent of each bone's local rotation measures the limits instead of assuming them. A knee's tracks only ever bend it one way, so the cone that comes out is narrow and centred on a half-bent pose; a shoulder's are wide and centred near its rest.

The cone is deliberately widened past what was measured. A clip shows what a living body does, and a dead one goes further than that — the margin is the difference between a limit and a demonstration.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Game.Igi1.Physics.RagdollLimits.Margin
member.summary: How much wider than the measured range a joint is allowed to be.
member.remarks: Half as much again. The clips show a living body's working range; a corpse exceeds it, and a limit set exactly at what was demonstrated would make every fall look braced.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Game.Igi1.Physics.RagdollLimits.MinimumSwing
member.summary: The narrowest cone a measurement may produce, in radians — 8°.
member.remarks: A bone that never moves in any clip measures a cone of zero, which would weld it to its parent. Some are genuinely rigid and should be nearly welded; none should be exactly so, because a solver cannot satisfy an exact weld and a joint at its limit every substep is a joint that jitters.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Game.Igi1.Physics.RagdollLimits.MaximumSwing
member.summary: The widest, in radians — 100°.

member.name: M:OpenIGI.Game.Igi1.Physics.RagdollLimits.Measure(OpenIGI.Formats.Animation.BoneAnimationSet)
member.summary: Measures every joint's range from the clips a rig ships with.
member.param: The animation set, whose skeleton the measurement is against.
member.returns: The limits.

remarks.para: A bone's local rotation is split into the swing that takes its own axis somewhere else and the twist that spins it about that axis, because a joint limits the two quite differently: an elbow swings through most of a half-circle and twists barely at all, and a wrist is the other way round. The split is the standard one — project the rotation's vector part onto the axis to get the twist, and whatever is left over is the swing.

The cone's axis is the average swung direction rather than the rest one. That is the part that matters for a knee: its clips never straighten it and never bend it forwards, so the average sits half-bent and the cone around it excludes straight and excludes forwards — which is a hinge, arrived at by measurement, with no bone named and no axis assumed.

member.name: M:OpenIGI.Game.Igi1.Physics.RagdollLimits.Decompose(OpenIGI.Core.Numerics.Quaternion32,OpenIGI.Core.Numerics.Vector3f)
member.summary: Splits a local rotation into how far it twists about an axis and where it puts that axis.
member.param: The bone's local rotation.
Its own axis, in its own frame, unit length.
member.returns: The twist angle in radians, and where the axis ends up.
member.remarks: The swing-twist decomposition: the part of the rotation's vector component along the axis is the twist, and what remains carries the axis somewhere else. Only the twist ANGLE and the swung DIRECTION are wanted here, and both come straight out without needing the swing quaternion itself.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Game.Igi1.Physics.RagdollSkeleton
member.summary: A rig prepared for the ragdoll solver: one rigid body per bone, with the capsule, mass, inertia and joint limits the constraint passes need.

remarks.para: Everything here is derived from the itself — no bone is named by index and no per-joint table is hand-authored. That is deliberate: the retail rigs' joint roles have not been measured, and this project does not guess at numbers it has not read. What the skeleton does state, and what turns out to be enough, is the tree and the rest translations.

A bone's origin is its joint, at one end of the limb it carries, so the body it stands for is the capsule reaching from there towards its children. That is why a centre of mass has to be carried separately: a rigid body rotates about its centre, and a bone does not sit at its own.
Build it once per skeleton and share it between every body wearing it; it holds no live state.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Game.Igi1.Physics.RagdollSkeleton.BodyMassInKilograms
member.summary: What a whole body is taken to weigh, in kilograms.
member.remarks: The masses are shared out by capsule volume and then scaled to this, so they are real kilograms and an impulse in newton-seconds means what it says. It also means the mass ratios come from the rig's own proportions rather than from a table someone wrote.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Game.Igi1.Physics.RagdollSkeleton.RadiusOfLength
member.summary: How thick a limb is relative to its length, as a fraction.
member.remarks: A limb's radius is a fraction of its own length rather than a constant, so a forearm is thinner than a thigh without either being measured. Clamped, because a rig has short bones that are not short limbs.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Game.Igi1.Physics.RagdollSkeleton.MinimumRadiusInUnits
member.summary: The thinnest a bone's capsule may be, in engine units — 4 cm.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Game.Igi1.Physics.RagdollSkeleton.MaximumRadiusInUnits
member.summary: The thickest, in engine units — 30 cm.
member.remarks: A torso really is this thick, and a solver that thinks it is not lets an arm fold through a chest.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Game.Igi1.Physics.RagdollSkeleton.ThicknessPercentile
member.summary: Which of a bone's vertices decides how thick it is, as a fraction from the axis outwards.
member.remarks: The seventieth percentile rather than the furthest vertex. A limb has outliers — a pocket, a buckle, the flare of a boot — and sizing the capsule to those makes every bone too fat to touch anything. Sizing it to the bulk of the mesh is what makes a chest a chest and a forearm a forearm.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Game.Igi1.Physics.RagdollSkeleton.InertiaFloorInUnits
member.summary: The smallest a bone is allowed to be for the purpose of its inertia, in engine units.

remarks.para: Ten centimetres. Inertia, not mass, is what makes a ragdoll come apart, and this is the fix. The generalized mass a constraint divides by is 1/m + (r × n)ᵀ I⁻¹ (r × n); when I is tiny that term dominates, and the correction that should have nudged a bone instead spins it — which breaks the joint it was trying to close, so the next pass corrects harder, and the body shakes itself to pieces on the first thing it touches.

A rig is full of bones with no length at all — a hand, a foot, the tip of the head — and those have the smallest inertia and the longest arms to their parents, which is the worst possible combination. Treating nothing as smaller than a fist is the standard remedy, and it matches the ten-centimetre floor mature engines document for dynamic bodies generally.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Game.Igi1.Physics.RagdollSkeleton.SelfCollisionSeparation
member.summary: How far apart two bones must be in the rig before they are tested against each other.
member.remarks: Two joints. One is too near — a bone and its parent are held together by the joint between them, and testing them as well would only fight it. Three turned out to be too far: it leaves out a forearm against a chest and a shin against a pelvis, which are exactly the pairs a folded corpse puts through one another.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Game.Igi1.Physics.RagdollSkeleton.DefaultSwingLimit
member.summary: How far a joint may swing off its rest direction by default, in radians.

remarks.para: Seventy degrees, and it is uniform because nothing has been measured that would justify anything else. A knee and a shoulder get the same cone here.

This is the honest weak point of the rig, and it is fixable by measurement rather than by invention — see , which reads the real range out of the animation corpus when one is available and leaves this as the fallback when it is not.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Game.Igi1.Physics.RagdollSkeleton.DefaultTwistLimit

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Game.Igi1.Physics.RagdollSkeleton.MaximumMassRatio
member.summary: The most a bone may outweigh the one it hangs off.
member.remarks: The single most effective thing that can be done to stop a ragdoll exploding, and it is not a solver change at all. A chain solved one joint at a time diverges when a light link has to move a heavy sub-tree, and a rig taken at face value is full of those — a hand weighs a fraction of the forearm it swings, and the pelvis outweighs the whole leg below it many times over. Squeezing every neighbouring pair into a narrow band removes the failure mode outright.

member.name: M:OpenIGI.Game.Igi1.Physics.RagdollSkeleton.Thickness(OpenIGI.Formats.Animation.BoneSkeleton,System.Collections.Generic.IReadOnlyList{OpenIGI.Core.Numerics.Vector3f},OpenIGI.Formats.World.MefModel)
member.summary: Measures how thick each bone is from the mesh it actually carries.
member.param: The hierarchy.
Each bone's own axis, unnormalized.
The skinned model, or .
member.returns: A radius per bone in engine units, or when there is nothing to measure.

remarks.para: Guessing this was the single worst assumption in the rig. A bone's thickness was taken as a fraction of its own length, which makes a torso — short bones carrying a wide body — into a stick, and a stick is something an arm folds straight through. It is also why a corpse read as having no volume: the shape the physics saw was nothing like the shape being drawn.

The model already knows. A skinned vertex is stored in its own bone's frame — that is why the skinner can transform it by the bone matrix with no inverse bind pose — so the distance from each vertex to its bone's axis is the body's real radius there, needing no bone to be named and no number to be invented.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Game.Igi1.Physics.RagdollWeapon
member.summary: The rigid body a held weapon becomes once the hand holding it is dead.

remarks.para: A weapon is drawn rigidly at a hand bone, which is right while the hand is animated and wrong the moment it is not: the rifle passes through whatever the corpse landed on, because nothing was ever testing it. Giving it a body of its own — a mass, a capsule and a joint back to the hand — is what lets it rest on the floor beside the body, or under it, the way a dropped weapon does.

It is one extra body in the same solver rather than a special case beside it. The ragdoll's arrays simply grow by one, its joint list by one, and every pass — integration, contacts, friction, self-collision — picks the weapon up without knowing it is a weapon.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Game.Igi1.Physics.RagdollWeapon.MassInKilograms
member.summary: What a held weapon is taken to weigh, in kilograms.
member.remarks: Four. Service rifles run from about three to five kilograms loaded, and the port has no weight in its own weapon data to read — the original never needed one, because nothing it models is ever pushed by a weapon's mass. Recorded as the invented number it is; what it has to be is heavy enough to swing the hand a little and light enough not to drag the arm.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Game.Igi1.Player.AnimTriggerRegistry
member.summary: The animation-trigger table: what an animation event id fires.

remarks.para: An animation's BOED events carry an id, a bone and a position. This table is what turns that id into something audible. It is filled by running animtrigger/animtrigger.qvm, which is nothing but 50 DefineAnimTrigger(eventId, taskType, resource, flag) calls — the same shape as .

Note what is not in it: event 1010, which is by far the commonest in the retail animation data. A table entry names one fixed sound, which cannot express a footstep whose sound depends on the ground — and the four walk_fence_* entries that are here are a specific surface. So the absence is consistent with 1010 being handled inside the engine.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Game.Igi1.Player.BinocularsView
member.summary: The binoculars' view and zoom, as Binocular_Use (0x470890) drives the view's field of view.

remarks.para: The handler writes the view's field-of-view tangent (HumanView+484) outright, and nothing between it and the screen smooths it: opening snaps it to the default, each zoom tick multiplies it by or , and closing snaps it home through the weapon change's view reset (0x4659E0). A zoom step is taken while the tangent is still short of its limit, and not clamped, so the last one may pass it by up to a step.

Alternate fire zooms too (Human+460 against last tick's +300): held, it zooms in; let go, it latches; pressed again while latched it snaps back to the default, and letting go of that press frees it to zoom in again. The dedicated zoom slots (+488 in, +492 out) zoom whatever the latch says.

The three angles are the weapon config's Binocular - Default/Max/Min FOV (degrees) tags, which 0x470D70 turns into half-angle tangents (default 70, 90 and 5 when a tag is missing) -- not the task's own arguments, whose reader halves with integer division and so makes the minimum 2 degrees, not 2.5.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Game.Igi1.Player.DragunovScope
member.summary: The Dragunov's sniper scope, as GunDRAGUNOV's fire handler drives it.

remarks.para: 0x472E50, read for this class, and a different machine from the MP5's sight: the latch lives on the view (+492, set by 0x4659D0, cleared by 0x4659E0), and it works like this. A rising edge of alternate fire opens the scope; while the key is still held the view glides in by a tick towards the weapon's own minimum tangent — release and the magnification holds where it is. The dedicated zoom slots adjust from there: resumes the glide in, glides back out by a tick, no wider than the default. A second press of alternate fire closes the scope and snaps both tangents home instantly — 0x4659E0 writes the defaults outright, where the MP5 glides out.

The edge detection is the input frame's own: the handler compares the alternate-fire slot's current value (Human+460, slot 7 of the newest frame at +432) against the previous tick's (+300, the same slot of the frame kept at +272). That the "keep zooming while held" behaviour falls out of the previous value being read is the original's own arithmetic, kept here.

While the scope is open the handler also multiplies the round's sampled view kick by before it reaches the accumulators — a braced rifle, not a different recoil model. The minimum comes from the TASKTYPE_GUNDRAGUNOV tail argument exactly as the MP5's does; the shipped 5 decodes to tan(2°) through the reader's integer halving. Changing weapons snaps the scope closed, as the weapon-change states do through 0x4659E0.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Game.Igi1.Player.ElectricFenceContact
member.summary: Retail electric-fence contact handling for the player.
member.remarks: Gameplay, not presentation: a damage factor, a cooldown and the zone the shock lands on. It sat among the renderers only because the code that calls it does, and it moved here — beside , whose zone it names — the first time that folder was audited rather than inherited.

remarks.para: The powered fence callback at 0x43FF70 dispatches to the HumanPlayer handler at 0x412F80. That handler selects zone 13, adds the HumanPlayer QVM argument-8 dose directly (retail 0.5; the player zone's multiplier is one), and writes a 45-tick guard. The player update decrements that guard once per tick through 0x4113C0.

The handler does not pass through generic hit damage or difficulty scaling, and it does not post a soldier ground-impact event. Keeping the rule here makes that behavior regressible without broadening the desktop game's private mission bootstrap into a test API.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Game.Igi1.Player.HumanBodyOffset
member.summary: The two body offsets locomotion state 44 drives — 0x40DFC0.

remarks.para: This is what consumes general arguments 4, 5 and 6 of DefineHumanPlayerGeneral, which had been named as "two 0.85 m distances and a 7-tick timer" without a consumer. They are not distances travelled: they are the range of two offsets and the time either takes to cover it.

State 44's entry (0x40DF70) is the ordinary three-line shape — play a clip, install the per-tick — except that it plays animation 19 when the crouch byte Human+829 is set and the state's own clip otherwise. Its per-tick then eases two floats on the model instance at Human+1260:

item.description: Sideways (model+412), toward ± while the strafe slots are held and back to zero when they are not. Always live.
Forward (model+420), toward while forward is held — but only while crouched. Standing, this axis is not touched at all.

remarks.para: Both ease at range / per tick, and the rate is recomputed on the edge — the tick the key goes down, or the tick the last one comes up — from the previous input frame at Human+272 against the current at +432. Retail: 0.85 m either way, reached in 7 ticks, so a quarter of a second.

What the offsets do to the body is not established. They are written to the model instance, not to the human's position, and what reads model+412 and +420 has not been traced. A lean is what a 0.85 m sideways offset gated behind a crouch looks like, and state 44 sits among the self-driving interactive states — but that is an inference and it is recorded as one. The easing itself is transcribed exactly.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Game.Igi1.Player.HumanBodyTurn
member.summary: How a human on foot turns on the input frame: the body's yaw (0x4610C0, float 0) or the view's pitch (0x464800, float 1).

remarks.para: The frame carries the angle as a fraction of a half-turn. A small value is divided by 2 - 16.67|s|, so once the input is under 0.06 (about 10.8 degrees) each tick takes roughly half of what is left.

Both halves average this tick's value with the last tick's when the view's scale (view+484) equals tan(pi/4) -- and only the pitch ever does. 0x464800 rounds the tangent to a float, 1.0, which an unzoomed view's scale is; 0x4610C0 compares against the FPU's own fptan of the float-rounded pi/4, 1.0000000437, which no float equals. Probed on mission 4: patrol 411 turned 62 degrees whole on its first walking tick, and an 8.5-degree error took 7.08 (8.5 / 1.21) with no half-step before it.
An AI clamps the angle before it writes it: to pi for walking and combat, which leaves only the easing, and to 0.0259 rad for a patrol's LookAtNode, which turns it at about 24 degrees a second.

member.param: Whether this half averages with the last tick: the pitch, not the yaw.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Game.Igi1.Player.HumanCameraMode
member.summary: The five modes HumanCamera dispatches on.

remarks.para: The camera does not own its mode. Its update sends the human a message carrying camera+112 as the payload, and Human's handler (0x45FCD0) fills that payload in — position, orientation, both field-of-view tangents, and at payload+112 — which is camera+224 — the mode. So the mode is pushed by the human, and nothing ever writes the camera's field directly, which is why searching for a writer of that offset finds nothing.

Its default source is Human+1264, set to at construction (0x45ECD0) and changed through one setter (0x463760). Every name below comes from either that setter's callers or from the handler's own overrides.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Game.Igi1.Player.HumanIdleTransitions
member.summary: The transitions out of locomotion state 0 — the machine's initial state.

remarks.para: From 0x4087B0, the per-tick function state 0's entry installs. It is nothing but an ordered chain of flag tests, each of which does the same five things: record the previous state, set the new one, install its function, and call that function immediately — a transition takes effect within the same tick, not the next.
Order is the whole specification: losing the ground beats everything, death beats movement, and the jump edge is tested near the end.

member.summary: Takes a crossing of rung event 8, unless it is the event time the climb last took.
member.param: The crossed event's authored time.
member.returns: when the crossing counts: state 37 then pauses and commits the rung, and all three states sound it and post the AI event.

remarks.para: 0x40D6B0, 0x40D920 and 0x40DA80 all open with if (Human+1336 == 8 && Human+1344 != Human+3464) and then store the time. Three behaviours follow from that one comparison:

list.item: The mount is heard. State 37's entry sets the latch to -1.0 and starts animation 168 afresh, whose first tick reports its event at time zero, so climbing on — from the foot, or at the end of the top mount — plays a rung sound with nothing committed.
A rung can be reversed. Paused just past the event at 1737, the first tick back crosses 1737 again; being the latched time it is ignored, and the clip runs back to zero.
Climbing off the top can start silently. Animation 170's first event is at zero; if the last rung climbed was also the one at zero, that first crossing is the latched time.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Game.Igi1.Player.HumanLandingViewKick
member.summary: The dip the camera makes on landing — installed by the fall, played out by the camera.

remarks.para: Two functions own this between them. The airborne integrator at 0x408460 ends a fall by calling 0x4659B0(camera, amplitude), which is the whole of the arming — one store of the amplitude to camera+452 and one zeroing of the phase at camera+456. The camera update at 0x464BD0 then plays it:

So it is not a damped spring, and it does not oscillate: it is a single half period of a sine. The phase walks 0 to π in steps of 0.20943952 — π/15, so fifteen ticks, half a second at the 30 Hz tick. The amplitude is negative ( at the clamp, a quarter of a metre), which puts the trough at the midpoint and brings the view back to where it started without ever rising above it.

The sine is sampled before the phase steps, so a landing's first tick shows sin(0) — nothing — and its last shows sin(14π/15) rather than sin(π); the amplitude is dropped on the step that reaches π. Landing again mid-dip restarts the phase from zero, because that is all the two stores in 0x4659B0 can do.

The camera offset is applied in world Z, not along the view direction: 0x464BD0 adds it to the same accumulator that carries camera+420, which lands on the position's Z component directly while the X and Y offsets beside it are rotated into the camera's basis first.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Game.Igi1.Player.HumanLandingViewKick.PhaseStepRadians

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Game.Igi1.Player.HumanLocomotionTriggers
member.summary: The two triggers the locomotion state machine watches — both of them double-taps.

remarks.para: HumanPlayer's constructor registers the locomotion machine with two triggers and the table at 0x538710. Each trigger is four steps of twelve bytes, and the two step arrays sit immediately before the trigger array and end exactly where it begins — 0x5386B0, 0x5386E0, 0x538710 — which is what fixes both the step count and the record size.

Both have the same shape over a single mask bit: set, clear, set, clear, with a tolerance of on each step after the first. That is a double-tap recogniser, and the tolerance is the window each phase must complete in.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Game.Igi1.Player.HumanLocomotionTriggers.Count
member.summary: The number of triggers the locomotion machine registers.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Game.Igi1.Player.HumanLocomotionTriggers.FirstMask
member.summary: The flag bit the first trigger watches — action bit 0x200.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Game.Igi1.Player.HumanLocomotionTriggers.SecondMask
member.summary: The flag bit the second trigger watches — action bit 0x80000.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Game.Igi1.Player.HumanLocomotionTriggers.WindowTicks

member.remarks: Each phase of the gesture has this long to complete. Hold the button past it and the trigger resets; tap again too late and it resets. The first step carries a tolerance of zero because nothing has started yet, and a mismatch on step 0 costs nothing.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Game.Igi1.Player.HumanLocomotionWeaponActions
member.summary: Which weapon action each locomotion state asks the torso to play.

remarks.para: Twenty-six of the forty-nine locomotion state entries call sub_413A60(human, action), which writes Human+3420 — the requested weapon action. The weapon machine's Ready state reads it back and dispatches whenever it differs from what is playing (Human+3416), which is how walking with a rifle plays the rifle's walk clip without the two machines knowing about each other.

This table is why states 9–16 are the walking set. An earlier pass read the locomotion flag 0x40000 as crouch, which would make 9–16 the crouched states. They declare and 1–8 declare , and the crouched states are 19 through 27 — reached through a different bit entirely. The binding table names 0x40000 , and this table agrees with it from a completely different direction.

member.summary: Declares the WEAPON_ID_* and AMMO_ID_* symbols the script resolves against.
member.remarks: Divergence, deliberate and temporary. The original does not register these names at all: 0x47CF20 registers the wildcard "AMMO_ID_.*" with the script symbol system and the weapon roster supplies the values as it is read, so the numbers depend on the order weaponconfig.qsc and the per-weapon scripts load. None of that exists yet, so any symbol this script names that is not already registered gets an id allocated in symbol-table order and recorded in . The ids are therefore not the original's; only their identity across the four natives is meaningful until M9 lands the weapon system. Nothing here overwrites an id a caller has already registered.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Game.Igi1.Player.HumanPlayerDeath
member.summary: What happens to the player when the last round lands — locomotion state 47, entered on the same flag the soldier's death state is.

remarks.para: The state's entry is 0x40E560, and the "player_death_" string in it is what names it. It does seven things, in this order:
remarks.code: human[829] = 0; // stand up out of any crouch row = sub_489E10(human + 596, human[744]); // the hit-zone row for the LAST ZONE STRUCK clip = row[8 + 4*rand(2)]; // ReactionA or ReactionB sub_4D61D0(human + 104, 0, clip, 0, 0.2); // play it on the whole body, blend 0.2 s ... stop the weapon, drop the view, release the aim ... sub_4638A0(human, "player_death_", 3); // one of three death sounds human[1636..] = human[1672..]; // velocity from the committed move
remarks.para: It is the same rule the soldier's general death state uses. 0x45C440 reads row + 4*rand(2) + 8 for a head or neck hit; the player reads it for whatever zone was struck. So a player shot in the leg falls differently from one shot in the chest, and the pair of clips per zone is what the hit-zone table's trailing two integers are for ().
The retail player table's reactions are 201/202 for the limbs and torso, 215 for the rear, 112 for the head and 204 for the neck — so five distinct ways to go down, chosen by where the round landed.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Game.Igi1.Player.HumanPlayerDeath.State

member.remarks: Forty-seven, and one of the nine the state-to-animation table marks self-driven — it names its clip itself rather than taking one from the table, which is precisely what choosing between two reactions requires.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Game.Igi1.Player.HumanUpperBody
member.summary: The torso half of a human's rig — the bone the weapon animations play on, and the bend that makes a body drawn from outside look where its owner is looking.

remarks.para: Every human skeleton the game ships (000, 001, 002, 003, 006) has the same 33-bone hierarchy, and it groups as: bones 0–3 the pelvis and spine, 4–7 the neck and head off the spine top, 8–13 and 14–19 the two arms off the spine top, 20–22 the weapon chain off spine bone 1, and 23–27 and 28–32 the two legs off the root (measured over 535 skinned bodies).

That shape is why the split is on and could not be anywhere else. Bone 1's subtree is exactly the torso, the head, both arms and the held weapon; everything outside it is the pelvis and the legs. So an upper-body clip on bone 1 and a locomotion clip on bone 0 divide the body along the line the animations were authored for, with no masking and nothing to tune.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Game.Igi1.Player.HumanUpperBody.Bone
member.summary: The bone a weapon's UpperBody* clip plays on.
member.remarks: The literal 1 in 0x489ED0: sub_4D6130(human+104, 1, 5, human+1616, id, loop, blend). Bone, orientation type, orientation source — and the only call to that function in the whole executable, which is how the upper-body track is known to be this bone and no other.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Game.Igi1.Player.HumanViewShake
member.summary: The shake a hit puts in the player's view — installed by the hit, played out by the camera.

remarks.para: 0x465970(camera, position, angle, ticks) arms it: an intensity of 1 at camera+436, the two amplitudes at +440/+444 and a fade rate of 1/ticks at +448. The camera update (0x464BD0) then plays it every tick while the intensity is not zero:
remarks.code: pitch += angle * I * u; roll = angle * I * u; yaw += angle * I * u; // three draws, in that order eye.x += position * I * u; eye.z += position * I * u; // then two more I -= rate (towards zero, clamped at it)
remarks.para: Each u is a fresh draw in [-1, 1), so the view jitters rather than swings, and the jitter fades linearly to nothing over the installed ticks. The eye offset is along the view's own horizontal right axis and along world Z. A bullet or a blow installs up to 5 cm and 0.75 degrees for fifteen ticks (0x412440, 0x412CE0), an electric fence the full amount for 45, and a blast its share for the explosion's own duration (0x412990).

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Game.Igi1.Player.PlayerCamera
member.summary: Drives a from the keyboard and mouse, and gives the renderer its eye.

remarks.para: The counterpart to FreeCamera: where that flies, this one walks. It advances the body on the fixed thirty-hertz tick rather than on real elapsed time, because the body's motion is the game's own and has to stay deterministic — only the look is taken per frame, so the view stays smooth at any frame rate.

Movement is root motion, from the animation. There is no speed constant anywhere: the input picks a locomotion state, the state names an animation, and the animation's root-motion track says how far the body moved. Changing the animation changes the speed, which is how the original works.

The work is shared out: is the look and the eye, settles what the weapons fire, and and run the states that own locomotion. This class keeps HumanPlayer_Update's order and the surface the host drives.

member.content: The remaster's weapon wheel over what the player carries.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Game.Igi1.Player.PlayerCamera.WalkDeltaPerTick
member.summary: The delta translation a walk covers in one tick, in the body's frame.
member.remarks: Divergence, temporary. The animation carries this in retail. Chosen here so the two speeds are a plausible walk and run — about 2.2 and 5.5 metres a second once the of 1.75 is applied.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Game.Igi1.Player.PlayerCamera.UnitsPerMetre
member.summary: World units in a metre.
member.remarks: The body works in the game's own integral world units, because that is what the collision octree indexes and what every constant read out of the executable is expressed in. The renderer works in metres. This is where the two meet, and keeping the conversion in one place is what stops a unit mistake reaching the physics.

The level's terrain.

remarks.para: The order is HumanPlayer_Update's, and it is load-bearing in two places. The weapon machine runs before the rig's clips advance, so it sees the clip-end flag as of the last advance — which is what makes "the animation has finished" a one-tick-late signal in the original too. And the trigger message goes to the gun after the rig has been placed, because the muzzle is this tick's eye.

member.name: M:OpenIGI.Game.Igi1.Player.PlayerFirstPersonView.HoldStill
member.summary: Lets the pointer go and drops the presentation's tick pairs, for a frozen frame.

remarks.para: What the pause menu needs of the player, and only that: the body is not moved, nothing is placed again, and the mission is left exactly where it stood.

The mouse is released because claims the cursor unconditionally — a first-person view looks wherever the mouse goes — so a menu drawn over it would be unreachable. Clearing the capture also re-arms the settling frame, which is what stops the warp that re-capturing produces on resume from arriving as a movement the player never made.

The tick pairs go with it, because a pair kept across the menu is a pair whose two halves are on either side of it: the first frame after resuming would draw the view somewhere between the tick before the pause and the tick after it. Dropping them makes the next tick build a fresh pair from where the player still is, at the cost of one tick drawn unsmoothed.

member.name: M:OpenIGI.Game.Igi1.Player.PlayerFirstPersonView.ReleaseLook
member.summary: Gives the pointer up without disturbing the presentation, and re-arms the settling frame.

remarks.para: For everything that takes the mouse away from the look but leaves the player standing where they were: the death camera's orbit, the third-person interaction camera, the map computer. Each of those drops the cursor lock, and dropping the lock makes the backend re-centre its virtual pointer — so the first motion after the lock comes back is a jump that has nothing to do with the player's hand. skips exactly one frame after this, which is what absorbs it.
Unlike the rig's tick pair is kept, because the player is still being drawn: dropping it here would cost a visibly unsmoothed frame every time the map computer closed.

member.name: M:OpenIGI.Game.Igi1.Player.PlayerInteractionDriver.ApplyRootMotion(OpenIGI.Core.Numerics.Vector3d,System.Boolean,System.Nullable{System.Single})
member.summary: Consumes this tick's authored root motion for a self-driving interaction.
member.param: The clip's world-space root step this tick.
Whether a non-looping clip reached its end this tick.

remarks.para: Fence animation 171 carries Jones across the obstacle in its root track, and the mover (0x4614B0) applies all three components of the step to the Human's origin -- the height included, which is how the origin rises over the fence. The body is drawn at that origin with the root's own height taken out (), as on a ladder. Keeping the task at its mount height and drawing the root height on top instead put the whole vault 0.96 m too high: the mount is already the origin, 3891.2 above the fence's base, and the clip's first root sample is 3938.6.

The step moved is the clip's PREVIOUS one. A clip node samples its root and takes the difference (0x4D4840) before it advances its clock (0x4D4B60), so the origin stands still on the update that mounts, and the frame on which the clip ends is never moved at all. Measured on mission 1's fence, retail's origin is the port's of one update before, tick for tick, and its fall starts with the second-to-last step, not the last.

member.param: The time of the step event (8) the clip crossed, if it crossed one.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Game.Igi1.Player.PlayerLoadout
member.summary: What a mission starts the player carrying.

remarks.para: Like the spawn point (), the original computes nothing here: the loadout is declared in the level's own objects.qvm, as child tasks of the HumanPlayer task. Level 1 builds them in this order:

So finding the loadout is finding those children — no heuristic, and the same answer the game uses. Task_DeclareParameters names both weapon arguments itself: ID as an EnumString32 and Slot as an Int16.

A weapon is recognised by its parameters, not by its type name. The script declares a separate task class per weapon family — Gun, GunMP5SD, GunDRAGUNOV, GunM16A2, Binocular — and the executable confirms why: GunMP5SD's constructor (0x473AB0) chains to Gun's and then hardcodes its own WEAPON_ID_MP5SD. Keying on an ID that starts with WEAPON_ID_ reads every family, including any this list has not seen.

Slot is not an inventory index and its meaning is open. Across all fourteen missions it is zero everywhere except level 1, where the Glock and the knife carry 1 and the MP5SD and binoculars carry 0. That is too little variation to name from data, and the parameter application in the executable has not been traced, so it is carried through unread rather than guessed at.

member.summary: The Gun* tasks a human carries, in the order its own child list holds them.
member.param: The human task — the player, or a HumanSoldier.

remarks.para: A soldier is armed exactly the same way the player is, and by the level author rather than by its AI type. Level 1's guards carry Task_New(-1, "Gun", "", "WEAPON_ID_AK47", 0) as a child of the HumanSoldier, beside the HumanAI, and the AK in AITYPE_PATROL_AK is part of the settings.qsc key rather than anything the engine resolves a model from.

Order is the whole selection rule. Everything that asks a human what it is holding takes slot 0 of the list at Human+1220 — the AI's combat per-tick (0x48B9C0, 0x48D8E0), the reload check (0x48B980) and the death state (0x45C440) all call sub_4F2060(human + 1220, 0). So the first gun child is the one in hand, and the Slot parameter is not what picks it: level 1 arms guards with a rifle and a grenade both declaring slot 0.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Game.Igi1.Player.PlayerLocomotion._running
member.summary: The walk/run latch. True is the retail default: the byte the toggle flips, HumanPlayer+3397, is zeroed by the constructor at 0x410370, and the flag word is built with if (byte) flags |= 0x40000; else flags &= ~0x40000 at 0x4105EA — so a zero byte means the walking bit is clear, which selects the running set, states 1–8. A player therefore spawns running and the first press of the toggle makes them walk.

member.name: P:OpenIGI.Game.Igi1.Player.PlayerShotResolver.TerrainTrace
member.summary: Gets or sets a trace through the terrain, for the casts a ground query cannot answer.
member.remarks: The view model's wall pullback sweeps forward, so it wants a ray through the terrain rather than the height under a point -- which is why it arrives as a cast the host supplies and not as something read off the ground the body stands on. A title whose terrain nothing can trace leaves this null, and the pullback then meets placed objects only.

member.name: P:OpenIGI.Game.Igi1.Player.PlayerShotResolver.AimConvergenceRay
member.summary: Gets or sets the ray the crosshair sits on — the drawn camera's own centre line.
member.value: The camera's position in engine units and its unit forward, or — the default, and the only value first person ever holds — to fire straight along the eye's own forward, exactly as the original does.

remarks.para: The one thing the third-person view changes about the game rather than about the picture. A camera behind and to the side of the eye does not share its sight line, so a fixed crosshair and a shot along the body's forward cannot both be right. Rather than let the crosshair wander to wherever the round would land — truthful, and unusable — the shot converges on what the middle of the screen is over.

A ray rather than a point, and this is the whole of the fix. Handing in a point meant the renderer decided what the crosshair was over, and it answered with a different test from the one the bullet uses — it saw walls and terrain and looked straight through people. So a shot aimed at a guard converged on the hillside behind him and landed half a metre wide, which is exactly the distance between the camera and the eye. Resolving the ray HERE settles it against and the same WorldTraceMask.World trace marches, so the crosshair's target and the round's target are found by one query and cannot disagree.

The round still leaves the eye: only its direction is turned, which keeps the muzzle, the tracer and the wall probe where they were. And the turn is the identity whenever the camera is at the eye, so first person needs no flag to be unaffected.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Game.Igi1.Player.PlayerShotResolver.AimConvergenceReachInUnits
member.summary: How far the convergence probe reaches, in engine units — 300 m.
member.remarks: Past this the angle between a shot from the eye and one from a camera 2.6 m behind it is a fraction of a degree. A ray that reaches the end unobstructed converges on the end, which is the same answer as not converging at all.

member.name: M:OpenIGI.Game.Igi1.Player.PlayerShotResolver.ResolveAimConvergence
member.summary: Finds what the crosshair is over, with the tests a round would meet on the way.
member.returns: The world point, in engine units, or when nothing is aimed.
member.remarks: The picking rule itself is , which is where the reasoning lives and where it is tested; this only names the three sources. They are the SAME ones a round meets: is what marches, is the cast through the ground the height field cannot answer, and is the reporting half of the cast it offers rounds to.

member.summary: Advances the ballistic rounds and lands whatever arrived this tick.
member.remarks: The impact side-effects are exactly 's, applied on the tick the round arrives rather than the tick it was fired: the hit counters, the AI's ground-impact notice and the decal. Damage needs nothing here — the delegate applied it during the cast, the same way it does for a ray.

member.name: M:OpenIGI.Game.Igi1.Player.PlayerShotResolver.ResolveShot(OpenIGI.Game.Weapons.GunProjectile,System.Single,OpenIGI.Game.Weapons.WeaponCategory,System.Single)
member.summary: Resolves one round the way 0x47B750 does — as a march, not a single cast.

remarks.para: The round is hit-scan and settled entirely in the tick it is fired, but it does not stop at the first thing it meets. The original loops while range is left, and each surface either stops the round, is penetrated, or deflects it — the rules are , which had been written from this same function and then never driven by anything.

Each surface's own row supplies the two numbers: against the weapon's penetration power (0x47BD88), and against the angle of arrival (0x47BB96). A deflection is allowed once per round and is tested BEFORE penetration, exactly as the original orders them, so a grazing round glances rather than punching through.

A crossing is an entry or an exit, never both: 0x4CD300 reports the two as the halves of one condition (*a7 = c0; *a8 = !c0), so the pair the trace hands back always has exactly one side set. An entry sounds and marks the surface and is what penetration and deflection are tested on; an exit leaves only the far-side decal, silently, and arms the latch that stops the round on its next entry (0x47BB0A) — which is what keeps a round that punched through a wall from carrying on through the whole level.

member.name: M:OpenIGI.Game.Igi1.Player.PlayerShotResolver.CommitMarks(System.Boolean)
member.summary: Marks the impacts one round recorded, with the flags the original gives them.
member.param: Whether the round glanced at any point.
member.remarks: 0x47C262: every impact is an exit once the round has glanced. Otherwise each is an entry except the last, which is an exit when its surface faced away from the round.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Game.Igi1.Player.PlayerShotResolver.KnifeFanRadians
member.summary: The blade angles KnifeStab tries, in order, in radians about the view's up axis.
member.remarks: 0x46DF70 starts at -0.2617994 (-15 degrees) and adds 0.17453294 (10 degrees) twice, stopping at the first angle that lands.

member.name: M:OpenIGI.Game.Igi1.Player.PlayerShotResolver.KnifeBladeDirection(OpenIGI.Core.Numerics.Vector3f,OpenIGI.Core.Numerics.Vector3f,System.Single)
member.summary: The direction of one blade angle.
member.param: The view's forward (+Y) axis.
The view's right (+X) axis.
The angle, in radians.
member.returns: The blade direction.
member.remarks: 0x4B3790 post-multiplies the view by the Z rotation 0x4B3BE0 builds, and the stab takes the result's middle column: cos a * forward - sin a * right. A negative angle therefore swings the blade to the right.

member.name: M:OpenIGI.Game.Igi1.Player.PlayerShotResolver.ResolveStab(OpenIGI.Game.Weapons.GunProjectile,OpenIGI.Core.Numerics.Vector3f,System.Single,OpenIGI.Game.Weapons.WeaponCategory)
member.summary: Resolves a knife stab the way KnifeStab (0x46DFB0) does.

remarks.para: The knife is not a gun ray. Its task sweeps the blade across , a cast at each, and hands the first thing that answers the hit message that message and nothing else: it never records an impact, so there is no GunShotEffect, no mark, no impact sound and no dust.

A body answers, so it ends the sweep. The port cannot ask a wall whether its type answers, so a wall does not end it; the first wall met is reported, flagged , only when no angle reached a body -- that is what lets a stab break a pane or silence a speaker.

remarks.para: The other half of every weapon action. 0x4137E0 picks a pair — a full-body clip for the first-person rig and an UpperBody* clip for the human's own body — and plays them on two different skeletons. Only the first is visible through the player's own eyes, which is why the second went unused here until there was a camera that could see the body.

Reported rather than played, because the body belongs to the renderer: this object owns the simulation's copy of what the torso was asked to do, and is how a consumer notices a new request without having to diff the id — a second shot plays the same clip again and must restart it.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Game.Igi1.Player.SoldierDeathFall
member.summary: 0x45D5B0 — the solver a soldier's death state runs to decide how far the body is allowed to travel while its death clip plays, and therefore where a corpse comes to rest.

remarks.para: A death animation carries real root motion: the body pitches forward or sideways over the clip. Played unchecked against a wall that is closer than the clip's stride, it would put the corpse inside the wall. The engine solves it once, at the moment of death, and returns a corrective velocity that the death state's per-tick (0x45C700) adds to the position every tick:
remarks.code: human.position += human[+3384] // three doubles, this function's output
remarks.para: The correction is always backwards along the clip's own motion, and never vertical. The arithmetic is what makes that work: over the clip's duration ticks the correction subtracts exactly the part of the stride the obstruction leaves no room for, so the body travels to the obstruction and stops. Nothing here makes a body fall — the drop is the death clip's own root motion plus the ordinary ground query.

Every constant is read from the disassembly at instruction level: 0x5333B8 = 4096.0f (the one-metre extension), 0x533430 = 2.0833334e-4f (one 4800th, the clip's duration unit), -3276.8f and +1638.4f (the ray heights), and 22.0 × 0.017453292 (the fan angle).

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Game.Igi1.Player.SoldierDeathFall.ExtensionInUnits
member.summary: How far past the clip's own stride the rays are cast — 0x5333B8, one metre.
member.remarks: The direction is rescaled so its length becomes stride + 4096, and that extended length is what the shortfall is measured against. So a body whose stride would end exactly against a wall is still corrected: the extra metre is the margin the solver keeps.

member.remarks: The order is heights outermost, angles innermost, starting at the lowest height and the leftmost angle — which is the order the ranking pass then walks, so it decides ties.

member.name: M:OpenIGI.Game.Igi1.Player.SoldierDeathFall.Direction(OpenIGI.Formats.Animation.BoneAnimation,System.Single,System.Double@)
member.summary: The clip's total root motion, flattened, extended by a metre and turned into world space.
member.param: The death clip.
The body's heading in radians about Z — Human+1292.
Receives the extended length, which the shortfall is measured against.
member.returns: The world-space direction, or a zero vector when the clip does not travel.
member.remarks: The vertical component is dropped, and it is dropped in an odd way. The first key's Z is overwritten with zero before the last key is sampled, and the delta's Z is then that zeroed slot negated — so it is always −0, whatever either key's Z was. Reproduced as written: the correction the solver returns is purely horizontal, which is consistent with it being a travel limiter rather than anything to do with falling.

member.summary: Runs the whole solver.
member.param: The death clip that is about to play.
The body's world position, in engine units.
The body's heading in radians about Z.
The world cast the nine rays go through.
member.returns: The corrective velocity in engine units per tick, to be added to the position every tick while the clip plays. A zero vector means "the clip may travel unchecked".

remarks.para: The fourth case is the odd one. When the obstruction is at exactly the ray's own origin — an exact three-way equality, not a tolerance — the correction is the whole direction, so the body ends the clip where it started. Everything between scales linearly by how far short the obstruction is.

member.name: M:OpenIGI.Game.Igi1.Player.SoldierDeathFall.RotateAboutZ(OpenIGI.Core.Numerics.Vector3d,System.Single)
member.summary: Turns a vector about Z, the way 0x4B3BE0's matrix is applied — rows dotted with the vector.
member.param: The vector.
The angle.
member.returns: The turned vector.
member.remarks: 0x4B3BE0 builds {cos, −sin, 0; sin, cos, 0; 0, 0, 1} and the caller applies it as M·v, which is the engine's other convention from Matrix3f.Transform. Applying it the wrong way round would place a corpse by the transpose of its own heading, which is a mirror image, so this is written out rather than routed through the helper that means the opposite.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Game.Igi1.Player.SoldierView
member.summary: A placed soldier's drawable state: the declared skeleton posed by the declared stand animation, facing the declared heading.

remarks.para: This is the soldier init handler (0x456E50) and the tail of Human's (0x45F890) without the scene graph. The original builds the bone object from the task's Bone Heirachy id (0x4D9620), plays its Stand Animation on bone 0 of the rig, resolves the ordinary Model parameter by name, and writes the facing as a pure Z rotation of Gamma into the object's own 3×3 (0x4B3BE0).

The pose is in the object's space with the facing baked in (0x4D38C0 builds the palette with a zero root position under the object's 3×3), so the world position is added by whoever draws it — the same convention as .

member.summary: Plays a weapon's UpperBody* clip on the torso, leaving the legs alone.
member.param: The upper-body animation id out of the weapon record.
Whether the clip repeats.
How long to cross-fade into it.
member.returns: when the clip resolved in this rig's set.

remarks.para: Bone 1, which is the whole of the split. 0x4137E0 picks one full-body and one upper-body id per weapon action; the full-body id goes to bone 0 of the first-person rig (0x489F20) and the upper-body id to bone 1 of the human's own skeleton-0 rig (0x489ED0 → 0x4D6130, with bone 1 written as a literal). So retail plays these on the body every time the player fires or reloads, invisibly — the data and the dispatch were always there, and the third-person view is only what makes them visible.

The split works because of how the rig is shaped: bones 0–3 are the pelvis and spine, the head and both arms hang off the spine top, the weapon chain 20–22 hangs off bone 1, and the two legs hang off the root. So bone 1's subtree is exactly torso, head, arms and weapon, and bone 0's clip keeps the legs.

member.name: P:OpenIGI.Game.Igi1.Player.SoldierView.UpperBodyAnimation

member.summary: Hands the torso back to the full-body clip on bone 0.
member.remarks: 0x489F00, which 0x4137E0 calls when the action is zero — the human is holding nothing and the upper body has no weapon clip to be in.

member.name: M:OpenIGI.Game.Igi1.Player.SoldierView.ReleaseUpperBody
member.summary: Gives the whole rig back to whatever is playing on bone 0.

remarks.para: An authored full-body clip owns the whole body. A ladder, a wire, a keypad and a death are each one clip that animates the character from the boots up, and they play on bone 0 — so a weapon stance still sitting on bone 1, or a spine still bent to an aim, replaces the half of that clip above the waist and leaves a man climbing a ladder in a rifle pose. Every one of those entries comes through here first.

A port decision, not a retail one, and it exists only because the port draws this body. Retail's bone 1 keeps its weapon clip through a climb, which costs it nothing: nobody ever sees the player's own body, and its own upper-body track is what the first-person arms are.

member.name: M:OpenIGI.Game.Igi1.Player.SoldierView.LookAlong(System.Single)
member.summary: Turns the body to look along its view's pitch — Human_ApplyLook (0x489F70).
member.param: The view's pitch, positive up; zero when the human's look is off.

remarks.para: Every palette rebuild (0x45F240) ends with it: bone 1 is turned by the pitch, up to 55° either way, about the body's own side axis, and whatever is left over turns bone 4 the same way. The view's yaw would turn them about the body's up as well, but only a target written by HumanView_SetTarget (0x465920) ever makes it other than zero, and its one caller clears it. A human looks this way from its creation until its body machine turns the look off.
Applied to every pose this rig builds, so the body drawn, the parts a round is tested against and the eye, gun and hand a soldier's brain reads all turn with it, as they do in the palette.

member.summary: Advances the rig by one tick.

remarks.para: Nothing called this before, and the pose was cached with ??= — so every soldier in the game stood frozen on the first frame its stand animation resolved to, which reads as a default A-pose. The clip has to be advanced and the cached pose dropped, exactly as the player's rig is.

member.name: P:OpenIGI.Game.Igi1.Player.SoldierView.LiteralDeathAnimations
member.summary: The two literal death animations, from the soldier class's two special death states — 0x45C5A0 plays 24 and 0x45C650 plays 25.

remarks.para: These are not the ordinary death clips, and using them was the floating-corpse bug. The soldier class has three death states — entries 32, 33 and 34 of its 38-state machine — and the third (0x45C440) is the general one, which works its id out from the killing weapon, the zone struck and which way the round came. is that function.

Measured over the retail sets: on skeleton 1, clip 24 starts from a crouch (root Z 2219 → 1020) and clip 25 is a 15-tick twitch already on the floor (462 → 523), while the clips the general state names — 22, 23, 28, 30, 71 — all run from the standing pelvis height of 3877 down to 524…772. So playing 24 or 25 on a guard who was standing left the body at standing height with a lying pose, which is exactly what a floating corpse looks like. Kept because the two literals are real; no longer what kills a guard.

member.name: P:OpenIGI.Game.Igi1.Player.SoldierView.RootSample
member.summary: Gets where the playing clip's own root-motion track currently puts the skeleton root, in engine units, in the body's model space — the original's Human+1300.

remarks.para: The soldier update calls sub_4D2FB0(human + 1300, human + 1312, human + 104) every tick, so +1300 is this and +1312 is the per-tick delta the mover consumes. 0x48A340 — which the AI's eye, the wall sweep and the ground query all locate a bone with — adds +1300 to the bone's rotated position, so a bone's true offset from the body's origin includes it.

It matters because a skeleton's rest translation for bone 0 is zero in every retail set, so the pose puts the pelvis at the object origin and the feet almost a metre below it. The root track's Z is what bridges that: 3877 units (0.95 m) standing, and 524…772 once a death clip has run. Only the Z is used here — the horizontal part is already carried by the body's own position, which the mover advances by the same track's delta, and a Z-only heading rotation leaves Z alone anyway.
