member.name: T:OpenIGI.Game.Igi1.Player.ThirdPersonCamera
member.summary: The over-the-shoulder view, and the move between it and the player's own eyes.

remarks.para: A remaster addition, and it says so. IGI1 has five camera modes () and none of them is a free third-person gameplay view; the two the port already draws from outside the body — the death camera and the ladder's mode 3 — are transcriptions, and this is not. Nothing here claims a retail address.

It changes only where the frame is rasterised from. The eye a round leaves, the ear the world is heard through, the wall probe, the aim angles and every tick of the simulation stay exactly where the first-person view put them: this takes the camera the player would have had and moves it back along that camera's own axes. Which is also what makes the transition cheap to get right — the orientation never changes, so there is no rotation to interpolate and no moment where the view is pointing somewhere neither mode would have.
The move itself is the feature. Three things make it read as a camera move rather than a cut:

list.item: The blend is smootherstep (6t⁵ − 15t⁴ + 10t³), whose first and second derivatives vanish at both ends. A linear blend starts and stops abruptly however long it takes, and plain smoothstep still steps in acceleration; this leaves and arrives at rest.

The camera travels an arc, not a line: the shoulder offset and the pull-back are separate legs of the same eased parameter, so the eye swings out past the shoulder rather than reversing straight out of the character's skull.

Reversing mid-move is continuous, because the blend is a position that is driven toward its target rather than an animation that is restarted. Tapping the key twice quickly makes the camera turn around where it is.

remarks.para: Collision is two rays and one asymmetry. The lateral leg and the pull-back leg are cast separately, so a camera pressed sideways into a wall gives up its shoulder offset before it gives up its distance. The limit snaps in and eases out: a wall arriving must take effect on the frame it arrives or the near plane cuts through it, while a wall leaving must be released over a few tenths of a second or every doorway fires the camera backwards.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Game.Igi1.Player.ThirdPersonCamera.UnitsPerMetre

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Game.Igi1.Player.ThirdPersonCamera.CollisionMarginInMetres
member.summary: How far short of blocking geometry the eye is held, in metres.
member.remarks: A ray finds the point a wall is at; the camera needs the point at which the wall is not yet inside its near plane. At the 90° horizontal field of view the world is drawn with, the near plane's own half-diagonal is about 0.16 m, so this is that with room for the rest of the frustum to clear a corner the single ray never tested.

member.remarks: The gate for everything the rest of the frame has to do differently — drawing the body, standing the arms down, projecting the crosshair. It stays true for the whole of the move back, which is what keeps the body on screen until the camera has actually arrived at the eye.

member.name: P:OpenIGI.Game.Igi1.Player.ThirdPersonCamera.OffsetInMetres
member.summary: Gets how far the camera ended up from the eye it was built off, in metres.
member.remarks: The measure the view model and the body are switched on by, rather than the blend: a camera whose pull-back a wall has taken away is at the eye however far through the move it is, and putting a character's head there would fill the screen with the inside of it.

member.name: P:OpenIGI.Game.Igi1.Player.ThirdPersonCamera.Camera
member.summary: Gets the eye the scene is drawn from.

member.name: P:OpenIGI.Game.Igi1.Player.ThirdPersonCamera.ShowsBody
member.summary: Gets whether the character should be drawn this frame.

remarks.para: A distance with hysteresis, not a share of the move. The distance because a camera whose pull-back a wall has taken away is at the eye however far through the move it is, and a head drawn there is the inside of a skull filling the screen. The hysteresis because that distance is decided partly by geometry: standing with your back a couple of feet from a wall puts the camera right at the threshold, and a bare comparison would flicker the character in and out as the player shuffled.

Which also gives the view a graceful floor. Backed hard into a corner the camera has nowhere to go, comes back true and false, and the frame is simply the first-person one until there is room again — rather than a close-up of the inside of the player's own head.

member.name: P:OpenIGI.Game.Igi1.Player.ThirdPersonCamera.ShowsViewModel
member.summary: Gets whether the first-person arms and their weapon should be drawn this frame.
member.remarks: Its own threshold rather than the complement of : the arms are anchored to the eye and are unusable long before a head is far enough away to be worth drawing. Between the two the frame shows neither, which at the default blend lasts about a twentieth of a second.

member.name: M:OpenIGI.Game.Igi1.Player.ThirdPersonCamera.Reset
member.summary: Puts the camera back at the player's eye at once, with no move.
member.remarks: For the cuts the blend must not smooth over: a level change, a spawn, a cutscene taking the view. Interpolating across one of those draws the frame from a line between two unrelated places.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Game.Igi1.Weapons.AimBasis
member.summary: Turns a shot's aiming frame to point at a place, without disturbing anything else about it.

remarks.para: A human fires along the middle column of its view's 3×3 (0x462E50), with the spread cone opening across the other two. That is exactly right when the eye and the camera are the same point, which in the original they always are. A third-person camera sits behind and to the side of the eye and so has a different sight line, and no fixed crosshair can be true of both — so the shot is turned to agree with the camera instead of the crosshair being moved to agree with the shot.

This is deliberately the whole of that change, in one place, so it can be read and so it can be shown to be inert everywhere else: with no target, or with a target on the eye's own forward, returns the basis it was handed unchanged.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Game.Igi1.Weapons.AimBasis.MinimumReachInUnits
member.summary: How far in front of the eye a convergence target must be, in engine units.
member.remarks: Half a metre. The camera traces from behind the player, so it can meet a wall the player is backed against — a point beside or behind the eye — and pointing the shot at that would fire the round sideways or into the player's own back. Anything nearer than this is refused and the shot keeps the eye's own forward, which is the first-person answer and always a safe one.

member.name: M:OpenIGI.Game.Igi1.Weapons.AimBasis.Converge(OpenIGI.Core.Numerics.Vector3d,System.Nullable{OpenIGI.Core.Numerics.Vector3d},OpenIGI.Core.Numerics.Vector3f@,OpenIGI.Core.Numerics.Vector3f@,OpenIGI.Core.Numerics.Vector3f@)
member.summary: Points an aiming frame at a world position, keeping its roll.
member.param: Where the round leaves, in engine units. Not moved.
The world point to converge on, or to leave the frame alone.
The barrel axis, turned onto the target.
The cone's first axis, re-squared against the new forward.
The cone's second axis, rebuilt from the other two.
member.returns: when the frame was actually turned.

remarks.para: The two cone axes are re-squared rather than rebuilt from scratch — Gram-Schmidt against the new forward, then a cross product — so the frame keeps the roll it had and stays right-handed. Building them from a world up instead would spin the spread pattern about the barrel as the player looked around, which is not visible in a round but is in a shotgun.

Every refusal path leaves all three arguments exactly as they arrived: no target, a degenerate one, a target too close, or a target so nearly on the existing forward that squaring the frame would divide by nothing.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Game.Igi1.Weapons.AimConvergence
member.summary: Works out what a crosshair is over, so a shot fired from somewhere else can be pointed at it.

remarks.para: A third-person camera does not share the eye's sight line, so the round has to be turned onto whatever the middle of the screen covers ( does the turning). This is the other half: finding that thing.

It has to look for the same things a round would meet. The first attempt asked the renderer, whose wall query sees placed objects and terrain and looks straight through people — so every shot aimed at a guard converged on whatever stood behind him and landed the camera's own half metre wide. Aiming at a person is the whole game, so a convergence that cannot see people is not a convergence. Three sources, nearest wins:

list.item: the placed objects, through the same query a round marches;
the terrain, which the object index deliberately does not carry and which is most of what a player aims at outdoors;
the humans, through the non-damaging probe — this is a sight line, and looking down it must not hurt anybody.

remarks.para: A ray that meets none of them keeps its far end, where the turn is a fraction of a degree and so is no turn at all.

member.name: M:OpenIGI.Game.Igi1.Weapons.AimConvergence.Resolve(OpenIGI.Core.Numerics.Vector3d,OpenIGI.Core.Numerics.Vector3f,System.Double,OpenIGI.Game.World.WorldTraceCast,OpenIGI.Game.World.WorldTraceCast,OpenIGI.Game.Player.HumanRayCast)
member.summary: Finds the nearest thing on a ray.
member.param: Where the ray starts — the camera, in engine units.
The ray's unit direction.
How far to look before giving up.
The placed-object trace, or for none.
The ground trace, or for none.
The non-damaging human probe, or for none.
member.returns: The nearest contact, or the ray's far end when it meets nothing.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Game.Igi1.Weapons.BulletImpact
member.summary: One surface a round met, and the mark it leaves.

remarks.para: The bullet resolution records up to of these as it works through a round's range, then spawns a decal for each once the round has stopped.

The bullet does not choose the mark. 0x4083C0 is a thin dispatcher: it packages the impact and sends it to a message slot on the material's own task type, so each surface decides what a hit on it looks like. A round through glass and into brick leaves two different marks without the shot knowing anything about either.

member.param: The struck surface's task type, which selects the handler. Taken from the hit object's own record — a different field for a human than for scenery.

member.name: M:OpenIGI.Game.Igi1.Weapons.BulletImpact.ClassifyEntry(System.Int32,System.Int32,System.Boolean,System.Single)
member.summary: Decides whether an impact reads as an entry or an exit.
member.param: Which impact this is, in the order they were recorded.
How many the round recorded in total.
Whether the round ricocheted at any point.
The surface normal dotted with the round's travel direction, for the last impact only.
member.returns: for an entry mark.

remarks.para: Three cases, in the original's order:

item.description: A round that deflected leaves EXIT marks throughout — the latch at 0x47C262 jumps straight to the exit answer for every surface a glancing round met, which on metal and concrete is the dent rather than the hole.
Every impact but the last is an entry, because the round demonstrably carried on past it.
The last impact is decided by the sign of the dot product: a normal facing the same way as the travel means the round was leaving, so it is an exit.

remarks.para: The sign test is > 0, so a normal exactly perpendicular to the travel counts as an entry.

The latch is read after the whole march. The original classifies its recorded impacts in a second pass, so a round that glances off its third surface retroactively turns the marks on the first two into dents as well. The live path marks each crossing as it happens and so reads the latch as it stood at that crossing; only a round that penetrated something and then glanced can tell the difference.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Game.Igi1.Weapons.FlashbangScreenFlash
member.summary: The first-person whiteout written by the retail flashbang player handler.

remarks.para: 0x00413090 writes two independent player fields: one for the hardcoded 25 metre visible range and one for the grenade's close radius. They fade independently in the player update; the renderer presents the stronger remaining value as a uniform white quad.
This class deliberately has no world-trace input. The native handler receives the flash event and compares its distance to the player's eye; it does not run a line-of-sight query.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Game.Igi1.Weapons.GunCasing
member.summary: The spent casing a round throws out, as the tail of Gun_Fire (0x478BA0) launches it.

remarks.para: A casing is only ever produced when the weapon names a and the gun belongs to the local player — the original compares the gun's owner against the player before doing any of this, so an AI soldier's brass is never simulated.

Both random draws are integers, and the speed conversion is integer arithmetic rather than the floating-point factor the player's movement uses. That is worth keeping: the same 4096000 / 108000 ratio appears in both places, but only one of them rounds.

member.remarks: An hour is 108000 ticks — 3600 seconds at 30 Hz.

member.name: M:OpenIGI.Game.Igi1.Weapons.GunCasing.SpeedInUnitsPerTick(System.Int32)
member.summary: Converts a whole speed in kilometres per hour to units per tick.
member.param: The speed.
member.returns: The speed in world units per tick, truncated.
member.remarks: Integer arithmetic, and the truncation is real. The multiply happens first and the division truncates, so 4 km/h gives 151 units per tick where the exact value is 151.7. The player's movement converts the same quantity in floating point and does not lose this, so the two paths genuinely disagree by a fraction of a unit.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Game.Igi1.Weapons.GunShotTracer
member.summary: One visible tracer a gun's GunShot task keeps: a 200-byte slot 0x47C4C0 fills.

remarks.para: A tracer is one PASS of a round's march, muzzle or step-off to contact or the range's end, filed when the march draws one. It lives until the task's render has drawn it once: 0x47ABD0 zeroes its life after the line, and 0x47C560 frees a zero life on the task's next tick. The thirty ticks it is filed with only matter while nothing draws it.

The two distances are cumulative over the round's DRAWN passes only (the march's running total grows only when it files one), and both are taken over the round's whole range, which is what the colour and the brightness run along.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Game.Igi1.Weapons.GunShotTask
member.summary: A gun's GunShot task: the rounds its fire handler queued, marched through the world in the task's own place in the level walk (0x47B690 to 0x47B750).

remarks.para: Every gun builds one when it is created (0x478540 to 0x47B110) under the level's dynamic container, so the tasks tick after the level's own objects, in the order the guns were made. A round fired in a soldier's update is therefore marched later the same tick, after every soldier has moved.

A pass casts from the round to the end of its range and takes the nearest contact. Coming out of a surface only latches the round, so the next thing it enters stops it. Going in, the struck object takes the hit, the material's sample sounds (inside its window), and then the surface decides: a glance (drawn whenever the round has not yet glanced, whatever the chance), or a bite of the round's power against the surface's resistance (drawn only on a tie). The bare level shell stops every round it does not turn.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Game.Igi1.Weapons.MeleeStrike
member.summary: How a close-combat strike books its damage.

remarks.para: A punch lands on hit zone 13 — the front torso, the same zone a shot from the front resolves to and the same one explosions and falls book to. Zones 12 through 14 all carry a 1.0 multiplier, so the choice is bookkeeping rather than arithmetic; 13 is the geometrically honest one for a face-to-face strike inside 1.5 metres.

The damage itself is the attacker's row CloseCombatDamage, already gated by CloseCombatHitProbability in AiPatrolCombat.RollMeleeStrike. Like a round's factor, it flows through the standard accumulator, so the player's difficulty scale applies unchanged.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Game.Igi1.World.AmbientAreaRegistry
member.summary: The level's authored ambience: the AmbientArea boxes that bed a sound in around the player.

remarks.para: The task is 528 bytes, registered at 0x44C130 with six parameters, and its update 0x44C370 is the whole behaviour. Mission 1 places beds like machinery room 02 and wind behind, each naming a sound definition.

The bed plays at the LISTENER, not at the box. The original sets the sound's position to the listener's every tick, so an area is a non-directional wash rather than a point source — which is what an ambience is. Its gain is the fade.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Game.Igi1.World.BloodEffects
member.summary: What a round does to a body — the mist, the droplets, and the marks both leave (0x463AD0 and its droplet callback 0x4640B0).

remarks.para: The Human class binds this to its damage message (0x45F94A, the very first thing 0x45F930 does), so every human takes it: guards, the player, and any body a round reaches. It is gated only on the blood game option, which 0x463AD9 reads before anything else.
Four things happen, and none of them depends on the surface the body is standing on:

item.description: The backstop mark. A trace runs on from the wound along the round's own line. If it lands on static world geometry whose material marks at all, one of hole_blood1.tex/hole_blood2.tex is stamped there at a radius of to twice that. This is the splash behind the target — which is why it appears on the wall a guard was standing in front of and nowhere else.
The mist. One blood1.spr quad at the wound, motionless, a third of a metre across, holding for ticks while its seven frames play, then gone in one more.
The forward spray. Three to five blood2.spr droplets into a ten-degree cone along the round's line, fast.
The back spray. Two to four droplets into a seventy-degree cone against it, slow — the splashback towards the shooter.

remarks.para: The droplets fall under a third of gravity and are traced against the world every sixteen ticks; where one lands facing the surface it stamps hole_blood3.tex or hole_blood4.tex and dies. So the pattern on the walls really is a function of the angle of the shot and where the body was standing — nothing about it is authored.

member.summary: Decides whether a landed droplet marks the surface it met.
member.param: Where the droplet's segment started, in world units.
Where it ended.
The surface it met.
member.returns: when the droplet marks.

remarks.para: 0x464178 takes start − end — the reverse of the droplet's travel — dots it with the struck face's normal and marks only when the result is negative. Equivalently: the droplet marks when it is travelling along the face's own normal.

Which way that face's normal points is the whole of the question, and it is settled by measurement rather than by convention. The original's normal is cross(v1 − v0, v2 − v0) (0x4CD300 through 0x4B3190) — bit for bit what computes from the same three vertices in the same order — and fanning rays into level one's geometry showed every first crossing has a positive facing. These meshes wind their normals INTO the solid, so travelling along the normal is travelling into the surface. A droplet that reaches the front of a wall splashes on it; one that caught the back of a face on its way out does not.

has already been turned to oppose the ray so that a decal sits proud of the surface, which is the opposite vector on an entry. The raw normal is recovered from , which is the sign the flip was taken from, and which the rich trace's carries too. Every droplet that reaches a surface from the outside is an entry and marks — what the shipped hole_blood3/4 textures are for.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Game.Igi1.World.GunShotImpactEffects
member.summary: What the GunShotEffect class (0x438440) does to a surface a round struck.

remarks.para: The bullet never chooses this. The shot march (0x47B750) records each crossing with the struck face's material row, and 0x4083C0 dispatches it to that row's own effect class. Every row in the retail data names TASKTYPE_GUNSHOTEFFECT, so this is what every impact runs, but the parameters are the material's: whether it puffs, whether it chips, which texture the mark uses and which model the chips are.
Three things happen, in this order, and each has its own gate:

item.description: Chips, when the block's second flag is set and the struck object is not a human. An Explosion0 is placed at the contact and fires once on its next tick (0x480F40), throwing instances of the block's model.
The mark, whenever the block resolved a texture — no flag guards it. This is ' business.
The puff, when the block's first flag is set, the struck object is not a human, and a coin comes up heads. Half of all wall hits therefore show no puff at all.

remarks.para: Retail's own table (material.qvm) sets both flags on every surface a round can mark except Glass, Fence, MetalLadder and MetalFence, and clears both on every second block — so the far side of a penetrated wall gets its mark and nothing else.

member.name: M:OpenIGI.Game.Igi1.World.GunShotImpactEffects.FragmentLaunch(OpenIGI.Core.Numerics.Vector3f,OpenIGI.Core.Numerics.IgiRandom)
member.summary: Draws one chip's launch velocity, as 0x47F4A5–0x47FF1B composes it.
member.param: The round's own travel direction.
The draw source.
member.returns: The velocity, in world units per tick.

remarks.para: The original draws the speed first, then a roll on [0, π), then a pitch on [0, cone), and that order is kept so every later draw in the tick lands on the same value.

0x4B4010 builds an orthonormal frame whose rows are u, w and the direction, where u = normalize(cross(s, d)) and w = normalize(cross(d, u)) for the horizontal helper s = normalize(d.y, −d.x, 0) — (0, 1, 0) when the direction is straight up or down. 0x47F515 then transposes it, so the direction becomes the third column, and the launch is that column after the frame is turned by Rz(roll)·Rx(pitch) on the right: cos p · d + sin p · (sin r · u − cos r · w).
The roll spans only half a turn, so the chips leave in a half-cone rather than a full one. That is the original's draw and it is kept.

member.name: M:OpenIGI.Game.Igi1.World.HumanVariantSound.Choose(System.String,System.Int32,OpenIGI.Core.Numerics.IgiRandom,System.Boolean)
member.summary: Builds the name one of the numbered variants is defined under.
member.param: The prefix, such as .
How many variants to draw between.
The engine's generator.
to reproduce the original's off-by-one exactly, as -vanilla requires; to draw the variants that actually exist.
member.returns: The definition name to play.

remarks.para: The original draws one name that was never defined. 0x4B47C0 is four instructions ending in an unsigned div, so the draw is [0, count-1] — while the definitions are numbered from one. So ai_death_0 and player_death_0 resolve to nothing and are silent, and ai_death_4 can never be drawn at all.
The near-identical sibling helper 0x4637C0 formats n + 1 from the same draw, which is what the correct call looks like — the same programmer wrote the + 1 there and left it out here.

This is a deliberate divergence, gated. Under the vanilla profile the port reproduces the silence, because -vanilla has to restore the original's mix. Otherwise it adds the one, which costs nothing and buys the fourth death sound the game shipped and never played.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Game.Igi1.World.Igi1Blasts
member.summary: The level's blasts as Project I.G.I. resolves them: grenades, rockets, launcher rounds, authored and vehicle explosions, and the rounds and blasts that break panes, set off barrels and shoot out speakers -- Explosion0's message to everything in its reach (0x47F200).
member.param: The mission's world.
What a blast does to the player when it kills.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Game.Igi1.World.Igi1ExplosionRuntime
member.summary: Project I.G.I.'s explosions as its simulation runs them: Explosion0 and what it leaves -- FireBalls, the smoke and the fragments -- on the engine's own random stream, in the order the original draws it.

remarks.para: The tasks are the ones both titles share (, , , ); the numbers are this title's. A blast lights its first FireBall for 75 ticks, a quarter smaller when others share it, and scatters the rest through its range, each lit 75/n ticks after the last and up to fourteen later; its smoke lasts 150 ticks, more when several FireBalls burn; its fragments fly for 45 ticks.

A fragment leaves along the blast's axis tipped by a draw of the cone (), not as the sequel throws it. A round's chips are explosions too, of no FireBalls (). The smoke's two puffs are particle systems of smoke2.spr on the impact effects' module, so the one particle drawer shows them.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Game.Igi1.World.Igi1GroundLight
member.summary: The light a Project I.G.I. level bakes into its ground, read at a point: what another game's rules see a human stand in, as I.G.I. 2 reads its own player's from the lightmap under its feet.

remarks.para: The level's data, not its picture: the terrain.lmp page the innermost TerrainLightMap cell over the point binds, its texel through the ramp the level's sun and terrain ambient build (). Every graphics preset -- the original's lightmaps, real-time light and lamps -- sees the same guards.

The two games' light is matched by what it shows. I.G.I. 2 stores a texel's light as a byte times 2/255 (Igi2TerrainVertex) and draws it doubled (MODULATE2X), so one shows the ground as bright as its texture and two twice as bright. Project I.G.I. multiplies its ground by the ramp's colour once (sub_5144E0, ZERO, SRCCOLOR): its brightest texel shows the texture as it is, I.G.I. 2's one. The ramp's brightness, nought to one, is the light as it is.

member.summary: A Project I.G.I. human as a world's lines and sight meet it: its hit test, answering the world's queries itself.

remarks.para: The world's line trace visits the humans along it (World_TraceLines, 0x4CC2A0), and Project I.G.I.'s human answers with its own handler (0x45F500): the evaluate first, then its body. This is that answer for a world that is not the human's own -- another game's, whose rounds and sight have to meet this game's player -- given the body as its hit test () casts against it, not its posed mesh.

The world says which query group the human is in and which of its materials a human is, so the answer reads as the world's own humans do: a line going into the body enters that material, one coming out of it leaves it.

member.summary: Holds the grenade cook tick for as long as the throw is charged.
member.remarks: The retail throw plays grenade_tick_1 once as it enters the throw state (0x40F590 calls sub_4E6B00 a single time) and stops it on release (0x40F640) — the audible cook while holding the pin. It is started once per charge and never re-triggered, and whether it loops is the sound's own to decide (sub_4E6B00 does not force it), not this caller's, non-positional like the rest of the player's own weapon sound.

member.name: M:OpenIGI.Game.Igi1.World.Igi1MissionAudio.PlayPlayerAnimationSounds
member.summary: Dispatches the sounds authored as events in the player's current view-model clip.
member.remarks: Reload sounds live in animtrigger/animtrigger.qvm, keyed by BOED event ids in the first-person weapon animations. They are therefore neither firing sounds nor weapon-record fields, and have to be tested after advances the rig.

member.name: M:OpenIGI.Game.Igi1.World.Igi1MissionAudio.PlayBinocularTransitionSound
member.summary: Maintains the retail binocular zoom motor cue while the operator is zooming.
member.remarks: COMMON/SOUNDS/SOUNDS.RES authors bin_zoom_1 as a loop. The retail device only makes this sound while a zoom key is actively changing the magnification -- not when the view is opened, and not while it settles to the authored default -- so it is driven off the player camera's BinocularZoomSteppingThisTick, and stopped the moment the zoom stops or the view closes. Keying it to the open edge instead played the cue every time the binoculars were raised.

member.name: M:OpenIGI.Game.Igi1.World.Igi1MissionAudio.PlayLadderStepSound(System.String,OpenIGI.Core.Numerics.Vector3d)
member.summary: Plays the rung sound of a ladder state's event 8 at the climbing human.
member.param: The definition name the climb took from its cycle.
Where the climber is, in world units.
member.remarks: 0x40D6B0 starts it under the sound root and then moves the voice to Human+32 (0x4E6C30) -- a positional one-shot, with neither the pitch spread nor the crouch scale a footstep gets.

member.name: M:OpenIGI.Game.Igi1.World.Igi1MissionAudio.TickLadderSlideSound(OpenIGI.Game.Igi1.Player.PlayerCamera)
member.summary: Starts, carries and stops the slide-down sound of ladder state 40.
member.param: The player, or when there is none.

remarks.para: The entry 0x40DBA0 starts wire_slide_1 as a child of the human itself and keeps the voice at Human+3508; the per-tick 0x40DBF0 stops it on the ground signal, in the same block that detaches from the ladder. Being the human's child, the voice falls with it, so here its position is moved every tick.
It is started once per slide, not whenever nothing is playing: should the definition be a one-shot that runs out before the ground, the original stays silent rather than starting it again.

member.summary: Stops the ladder slide's voice, at the ground or at a lifecycle boundary.

member.name: M:OpenIGI.Game.Igi1.World.Igi1MissionAudio.StopBinocularTransitionSound
member.summary: Stops the looping binocular cue when player ticking is suspended.
member.remarks: Death-camera and mission teardown deliberately stop ticking the player. Those paths therefore cannot rely on observing a closed-view edge on a later player tick; stop the voice at the lifecycle boundary instead.

member.name: M:OpenIGI.Game.Igi1.World.Igi1MissionAudio.PlayMedipackSound
member.summary: Plays the medipack's authored cue when its sustained syringe action starts.
member.remarks: IGI.EXE's medipack execution state consumes a charge and applies one heal after its damage and ammo checks, while the state keeps one syringe clip looping. The cue belongs to that action edge, not to every cooldown-eligible dose, so a fifty-charge pack cannot spam a sound each tick.

member.name: M:OpenIGI.Game.Igi1.World.Igi1MissionAudio.PlayGunPickupSound(OpenIGI.Game.World.GunPickup)
member.summary: Plays the retail world-weapon cue after a GunPickup reaches the player.

member.name: M:OpenIGI.Game.Igi1.World.Igi1MissionAudio.TakeGenericPickup(OpenIGI.Game.World.GenericPickup)
member.summary: Awards and plays an authored item that has reached the player.
member.returns: when it was ammunition, whose message the caller posts.

remarks.para: GenericPickup::cleanup calls 0x4E7200("pickup", 0, 0). The cue is shared by C4, keycards and every other GenericPickup; the model does not select a per-item sound. Like retail, it is played at the listener rather than at the item's former world position.
An AmmoPickup instead hands its ammunition to the player (0x46D990), whose handler adds it and plays weaponpickup_1 (0x45FF80); the box plays no cue of its own.

member.name: M:OpenIGI.Game.Igi1.World.Igi1MissionAudio.TickAmbience(OpenIGI.Core.Numerics.Vector3d)
member.summary: Advances the level's authored ambience and keeps its beds sounding.
member.param: Where the ear is, in engine units.
member.remarks: The beds are played flat, not positionally, because that is what the original does with them: it sets the sound's position to the listener's every tick, which is a wash around the player rather than a source in the world. Gain is the area's fade, so walking into a machine room brings its hum up over twenty ticks instead of switching it on at the doorway.

member.name: M:OpenIGI.Game.Igi1.World.Igi1MissionAudio.PlayJumpSound
member.summary: Plays the retail jump cue on the take-off tick.
member.remarks: Locomotion state 28's entry at 0x40BBF7 pushes "jump_1" (0x00536DC4) into 0x4DD750. Like the player's fall and death cues it belongs to the listener, so it is not world-panned.

member.name: M:OpenIGI.Game.Igi1.World.Igi1MissionAudio.PlayFootstep(OpenIGI.Game.Igi1.World.Footstep@)
member.summary: Plays a footstep where it landed.
member.param: The step, already resolved against the ground it landed on.
member.remarks: Pitched between 0.8 and 1.3, which is the whole of why two steps on the same surface are never quite the same sound. Low priority: a firefight is more worth a voice than a footfall.

member.name: M:OpenIGI.Game.Igi1.World.Igi1MissionAudio.PlayLandingSound(System.ValueTuple{System.String,OpenIGI.Core.Numerics.Vector3d})
member.summary: Plays the sound the ground itself makes when the player lands on it.
member.param: The definition name and where the feet touched down.
member.remarks: Flat: 0x40BE40 and 0x40BBD0 both start this voice and then leave it alone -- no pitch variation and no volume change, unlike a footstep. Priority sits above a footfall because a landing is a single deliberate event rather than one of a stream.

member.name: M:OpenIGI.Game.Igi1.World.Igi1MissionAudio.TickAlarmSpeakers
member.summary: Keeps every alarm speaker's siren matched to its own expression, positionally.

remarks.para: The retail speaker spawns a looping sound child at its own position the tick its expression turns true and destroys it the tick it turns false — so every siren in the level starts on the SAME tick and each is heard from the wall it hangs on. This is that behaviour through the port's voice pool: one held voice per sounding speaker, restarted if the bank's definition happens not to loop, stopped on the falling edge.
A destroyed task is removed immediately and its renderer selects the authored wreck model.

member.name: M:OpenIGI.Game.Igi1.World.Igi1MissionTick.UpdatePlayer
member.summary: The player's update: input, movement and the weapon, once per tick.
member.remarks: A dead player is in locomotion state 47, whose per-tick is not the walking one -- so the body stops being stepped rather than being stepped with no input. Without this a corpse walks around. What the update set in motion -- sounds, effects, detonations -- is resolved after the walk while holds.

member.name: M:OpenIGI.Game.Igi1.World.Igi1MissionTick.NotifyGrenadeAiEvents
member.summary: Delivers native grenade/explosion AI events before the soldier tick.
member.remarks: IGI1 broadcasts these from the task update itself: type 17 when a grenade is created, type 18 on the debounced landing sound, type 19 for a flashbang, and type 21 for an explosion. They are deliberately separate from gunshot/walk noise. The physics lists stay available until the effect pass below, so this method only consumes the one-shot throw list.

member.name: M:OpenIGI.Game.Igi1.World.Igi1MissionTick.AttachToLevelWalk(OpenIGI.Engine.Tasks.GameTask)
member.summary: Puts the soldiers (with their doors and alarms) and the player into the level's walk.
member.remarks: Retail updates HumanPlayer_0 where the walk reaches it inside ConditionalContainer_560, late in Dynamic: its HumanView, Shadow, then HumanPlayerInput, whose CHANNELS packet moves it, then the binoculars and the gun. A level without a player task keeps updating the player after the walk.
member.param: The level's task tree.

member.name: M:OpenIGI.Game.Igi1.World.Igi1MissionTick.StartLadderClimbAnimation(OpenIGI.Game.Igi1.Ai.ISoldierPresenter)
member.summary: Enters state 37's clip: animation 168's first frame, then held at the mount event.
member.param: The bodies, which draw the player's.

remarks.para: The entry 0x40D660 starts animation 168 as a new clip node: a full frame step forward (0x4D4F60), flagged 0x8000 so its first tick also reports the event at its start time (0x4D4B60). HumanPlayer_Update ticks that clip and moves the human by it in the same update, and the next update's state 37 finds event 8 at zero against the latch its entry cleared: it pauses the clip, commits nothing, and plays a rung sound. That is the sound of getting on — from the foot, or at the end of the top mount.
The port takes all of it here, in one go, so the pause is in place before any input can start a rung; otherwise the mount event would land on the first rung's tick and commit it.

member.name: M:OpenIGI.Game.Igi1.World.Igi1MissionTick.TakeLadderRungEvent(System.Nullable{System.Single})
member.summary: Sounds a ladder state's crossing of event 8, when the latch lets it count.
member.param: The crossed event's time, or null when the clip crossed none.
member.returns: when the crossing counted, so state 37 should commit its rung.

member.name: M:OpenIGI.Game.Igi1.World.Igi1MissionTick.ResolveStandInTick(OpenIGI.Game.Player.IHumanBodyState)
member.summary: What the mission's own player's tick would have stepped of the world, while another game's player stands in for it: the effects -- a shot camera's fireball, a barrel's -- the barrels' fuses, the alarm speakers and the security cameras' beeps and whirs, and the level's ambience where the stand-in listens from.
member.param: The player standing in.
member.remarks: steps these for the mission's own player among its own sounds and rounds; the stand-in's sounds, effects and rounds are its own game's, so only the world's half is stepped here, once a tick the stand-in ran. Without it a camera that has seen the stand-in glows red with no warning beep first, and anything that explodes stays on its first frame.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Game.Igi1.World.Igi1ObjectLight
member.summary: The light a Project I.G.I. level bakes into its buildings' floors, read where a human stands on one: indoors, as I.G.I. 2 reads its own player's from the lightmapped face under its feet.

remarks.para: The level's data, not its picture: each lightmapped model's own .olm pages (lightmaps/lightmaps.res), sampled at the lightmap coordinates of the face under the feet. Every graphics preset sees the same guards.

A line goes down from just above the feet; the first lightmapped face it meets is what the player stands on. Where it meets none, the player is on the ground or on something the level does not light, and answers. Models are taken where the level places them: a lift's floor is read where the lift starts.

A texel's light is its brightness as it is: Project I.G.I. multiplies its models by their lightmaps once, so its brightest texel shows a floor as bright as its texture, which is I.G.I. 2's one (a byte times 2/255, drawn doubled). See .

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Game.Igi1.World.Igi1SectorVisibility
member.summary: Project I.G.I.'s sector cull, decided once a frame from the eye: which buildings and rooms are drawn, and which objects outside the building the camera stands in.

remarks.para: Where the camera stands decides the frame. World_Draw (IGI.exe 0x4D2650) asks every building near the eye which of its sectors the eye is over, and draws the one that answers first (SectorObject_EnterHandler, 0x4DD310): walked from that sector through the whole screen, its shell drawn only if the walk reaches it. Reaching the shell is seeing out, and SectorObject_DrawSector (0x4DD5D0) then records the rectangle the shell was reached through as the outside's window.

Then the queue is emptied with that answer (QCube_CallHandlers, 0x4D12C0). An object whose origin stands within the building's optimal inside sphere () is drawn as ever. One beyond it is outside: drawn only once the walk has seen out, and only through the outside's window, which narrows the display area its own exclusion test measures against. That is the whole gate -- the ground is drawn outside it, unconditionally, and Project I.G.I. has no per-room test for the objects inside.
With the camera over no building, every building is walked from its shell through the whole screen, so its rooms are drawn only where its openings show them.

How Project I.G.I.'s walk differs from the sequel's. A sector already requested only widens its one rectangle and is not walked again (SectorObject_RequestSector, 0x4DD4B0), and a walk offers every sector of the building but the one it is looking out of (SectorObject_TraverseSector, 0x4DD650) -- there is no discard list, and no list of windows. Every portal is open: the building's sixty-four portal bytes are set to one as it is made (0x4DDF60) and nothing writes them again. Sector_IsPortalVisible is the sequel's ().

Clipped as well as culled. The display area the queue narrows for an outside object is what the rigid mesh's triangles are clipped against (0x4A0340, called from the mesh draw 0x49BE10), so such an object is drawn only within the outside's window (). The ground is drawn before the queue, through the whole display area, and is not.

The one type always outside never is. The queue also treats as outside any object of the type in word_C30064. Nothing in the binary writes it: it lies in the zero-filled tail of .data, and its only reference is that compare. So it holds type id nought, QTask itself (the first type 0x4010D0 registers), which no drawn object is, and the distance is the whole test.
Not reproduced. A building's level of detail is not consulted.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Game.Igi1.World.Igi1WorldBuilder
member.summary: Walks a Project I.G.I. level into placements.

remarks.para: A wrapper, and deliberately nothing more. is unchanged and still lives in the shared project beside the type it produces; what moved is who decides to call it. The host used to, which made the host a host only this game could load a mission into.

Its counts come back as nought because this walk does not keep them: it reports what it could not place through the log as it goes, rather than tallying. That is worth leaving alone — the numbers are for a developer overlay, and inventing them here would mean re-walking the scene to count what the walk already logged.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Game.Igi1.World.ImpactEffectRuntime
member.summary: Every particle effect a round produces, owned in one place and stepped on the fixed tick.

remarks.para: This is where the two dispatchers land. A surface hit runs the struck material's GunShotEffect block () — a puff of dust and a handful of chips; a body hit runs Human's blood () — a mist, two sprays of droplets, and the marks the spray leaves on whatever it reaches. The marks all go into the same the bullet holes do, because in the original they are the same kind of thing: a texture projected onto the object that was hit.

Blood systems belong to the body, not to the shot. The original stores them on the human, so a guard caught in a burst shows two mist quads and ten droplets no matter how many rounds land. That cap is the difference between a wounded guard and a fountain, so the systems are kept per owner here too and only released once both have gone quiet.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Game.Igi1.World.MefSkinner
member.summary: Poses a skinned model's vertices against a bone palette, as 0x49B700 does.

remarks.para: The rig is one bone per vertex plus a list of extra weighted influences, not a fixed four-weights-per-vertex layout. The source array is two runs — base vertices followed by extras — and the same 40 bytes are read two different ways: for a base vertex the trailing eight are { f32 scale, u16 _, u16 bone }, and for an extra they are { f32 weight, u16 target, u16 bone }.

Two details are the original's and would not be guessed. A base vertex's position is scaled by its own +32 float after the bone transform, and its normal is rotated but neither translated nor scaled. An extra influence is not scaled at all, and it accumulates only into the position — never the normal.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Game.Igi1.World.RetailTerrainRay
member.summary: The terrain half of the original's batch segment query, RayCast (0x4CC2A0), with its exact arithmetic: the answer a car's wheel rays get, bit for bit.

remarks.para: The original's terrain ray cast, step for step: one box over the whole batch fixes how deep the first ray's start is descended (0x4C9A30); from there each ray walks the octree depth first, nearest child first, admitting children by an integer box with ±16385 of vertical slack and a slab test (0x4CC810); the first leaf with a hit ends the walk; the leaf's triangles are tested with a float plane hit and a projected barycentric test (0x4CD300); a DiscardTerrain box around the hit point drops it (0x52BF00). Every operation is an one.

This is deliberately separate from , which serves gameplay rays: the two disagree on which hit wins when leaves overlap, and routing bullets through this one is a separate decision. On the levels that ship a terrain.hmp, a leaf inside a HeightMap task's cube has its vertices raised by that grid first, which is how the descent's enter hooks leave it.

member.summary: The five colours the level's FlatSky paints its dome with: the zenith, and a middle and a bottom pair that the dome blends between around each ring.
member.param: The zenith, SkyDome Top Colour.
The first of the middle pair.
The second of the middle pair.
The first of the horizon pair.
The second of the horizon pair.

remarks.para: This is the only place a Project I.G.I. level says what hour it is. Its Dirlight cannot: every mission authors that sun at a Time of 12, and the retail handlers registered by sub_526EE0 (0x526EE0) never read Time as a clock -- the sun is a bake-time light and a direction for the models with no lightmap. A night mission such as the third authors the same "noon" sun, 24° up and nearly white, as a daylit one. What the original DRAWS as night is this dome.
Snapping is applied as the dome builder applies it -- sub_51EB40 copies the second colour of each pair over the first -- so what is read here is what is painted.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Game.Igi1.World.TerrainChunkMesh
member.summary: Turns a chunk the traversal picked, plus its terrain.cmd block, into drawable geometry — the vertex and texturing half of sub_510010.

remarks.para: A chunk's vertices are one dword each: three 6-bit coordinates biased by 24, in units of a twenty-fourth of the chunk's extent. Unpacking them, applying the chunk's orientation and scaling by the extent puts them in world space, and the heightmap — where one is bound — displaces the finest levels on top of that.

The ground texture comes from three things at once. The level's TextureModifier layers decide which material covers each vertex; the material's band for this chunk's level of detail gives a scale and a tile map; and the tile map, indexed by three bits of the scaled world position, names one tile of terrain.tex. The same scale then walks the texture coordinate across the chunk, so a tile repeats every 256 steps and the 8×8 map cycles every 2048 — which is why the tile is constant over a chunk and the coordinates still line up with its neighbours.

Positions come out relative to the chunk's centre and in metres, so the geometry does not move as the camera does and can be uploaded once and drawn from . That is the same reuse the original gets from its render-chunk cache.

Two things the file does not settle are left alone rather than guessed at. The strip's winding alternates within a run and resets on the 0xF0 flag, but no reading of that rule makes a chunk's triangles face consistently, so indices are emitted exactly as written and terrain is drawn double-sided. And nothing in terrain data holds a normal, so the normal is zero — the mesh shader does not sample it.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Game.Igi1.World.TerrainChunkMesh.MaximumVertices
member.summary: The largest vertex index a triangle command can hold.
member.remarks: Indices are single bytes, which is why a block never carries more than 256 vertices.

member.remarks: The band's second scale uses one less, so it lays tiles at twice the density. Only the first is drawn here; the second is the detail layer the original cross-fades on top.

member.name: M:OpenIGI.Game.Igi1.World.TerrainChunkMesh.FillSurfaceNormals(OpenIGI.Core.Graphics.Vertex3D[],System.ReadOnlySpan{System.UInt16},System.Int32)
member.summary: Gives a layer's vertices a shading normal taken from the surface they describe.
member.param: Every vertex of the chunk; only this layer's slice is touched.
The layer's triangles, as vertex indices within the layer.
The slot this layer's vertices start at.

remarks.para: The terrain has no normal to give: the channel a mesh keeps one in carries the offset to where the vertex sits at the next level of detail, and the one beside it the texture offset that goes with it. A renderer that lights the ground with that offset gets a chequerboard — the offset swings smoothly from pointing up to pointing sideways across a chunk, and a surface lit by the cosine of its angle to the sun turns a smooth swing into a hard edge.

So the normal comes from the surface itself: the sum of the facing of every triangle meeting a vertex, weighted by area because a cross product's length is twice its triangle's. That is smooth across the chunk, where a normal taken per triangle in the pixel shader would be flat, and flat over triangles this size keeps the very patchwork it was meant to remove.
Every normal is turned to face upwards. The ground is a heightfield, so none of them legitimately points down, and the winding these triangles arrive with is not dependable.

member.name: M:OpenIGI.Game.Igi1.World.TerrainChunkMesh.ProjectVertex(OpenIGI.Game.Igi1.World.TerrainChunkMesh.ChunkProjection@,OpenIGI.Core.Numerics.Vector3d@,System.Int32,System.Int32)
member.summary: Builds one vertex's texture coordinate from its pass's projection.
member.remarks: The axis selector is authored in the node's own frame, so when the chunk's orientation swaps the X and Y axes the selector's choice of horizontal axis flips with it — the (swap ^ selector) & 1 in sub_512C30.

member.summary: Unpacks a block's vertices to chunk-relative offsets, computes each one's seam-morph target, and picks each one's material.
member.remarks: The morph is sub_512C30's: a vertex renders at own + morph · t, with t the LOD fade. An interpolated vertex's target is its source vertex's far position, so at distance it collapses onto the edge the coarser neighbour draws and the seam closes; a base vertex at the heightmap's threshold exponent carries the negated height, which fades the displacement in as the camera approaches (the original's separate fourth channel).

member.name: M:OpenIGI.Game.Igi1.World.TerrainChunkMesh.ReadTriangles(OpenIGI.Formats.World.TerrainCommandBlock@,System.Int32,System.Int32,System.UInt16[])
member.summary: Reads the triangle list with a consistent winding, dropping any triangle that leaves its own block.
member.remarks: The triples are uniformly wound as authored — over every block of level 1, 110554 shared edges run in opposite directions and none in the same — so they are emitted as written. The sign alternation in sub_512C30 compensates its own strip walk, which carries a continuation triangle's shared vertices in shifted register order; it is not a property of the data. What does flip winding is the orientation's mirror bit (the bit sub_512C30 publishes to 0xA7E06C as its cull seed): a reflected chunk's transformed triangles wind the other way, so its triples are emitted swapped and every chunk lands with the same facing.
member.param: The chunk's command block.
How many vertices the block holds, for rejecting out-of-range indices.
The chunk's orientation, whose mirror bit flips the winding.
Receives the indices; at least block.TriangleCount * 3 long.
member.returns: How many indices were written, which is short of the block's own count when it drops one.

member.remarks: The order is the drawing order, and it has to run from the material that covers the most to the one that covers the least — otherwise a patch would be painted over by the ground it sits on. A material's specificity is the layer that produced it, and the layers are already sorted with the smallest first, so the last layer to declare a material is the least specific place it comes from.

member.name: M:OpenIGI.Game.Igi1.World.TerrainChunkMesh.Project(OpenIGI.Game.World.TerrainChunk@,OpenIGI.Game.World.TerrainSurface,System.Int32,System.Boolean)
member.summary: Picks a chunk's tile and the texture coordinates that walk across it.
member.remarks: Everything here is per chunk, as it is in the original: the tile and the coordinate at the chunk's centre are computed once, and a vertex only adds its own offset times the rate. The rate is exactly the derivative of the origin with respect to position, which is what keeps the coordinates continuous from one chunk to the next even though each picks its own tile. The detail pass uses the band's second scale and tile map at one less shift, so its tiles repeat at twice the density; its rate divisor is the extent rather than twice the extent, which is the same doubling.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Game.Igi1.World.TerrainGeometryPool
member.summary: Recycles the vertex and index arrays a keeps.

remarks.para: A chunk's geometry outlives its build — the renderer re-reads it to re-append a rebuilt page — so it cannot be scratch. But it dies with the chunk, and a moving camera evicts chunks at the same rate it builds them, so the arrays one chunk gives up are the arrays the next one needs. At forty-eight bytes a vertex a chunk's vertices are routinely over the eighty-five kilobyte threshold, which put every build straight on the large object heap and every eviction's worth of them in front of a gen2 collection.

Buckets are keyed by exact length, never by "at least this long". Chunks at one level of detail share a vertex count, so exact keys still hit almost every time, and it means a recycled array is indistinguishable from a fresh one: Vertices.Length keeps meaning what it says, which is what the renderer divides by the layer count to recover a chunk's vertex count.
Nothing here is thread-safe; it belongs to the renderer that builds and evicts, on its own thread.

member.summary: How many arrays one length keeps before the rest are left to the collector.
member.remarks: A bound rather than a cache: the point is to serve the churn of a camera crossing the level, not to hold every chunk the player has ever walked past. Past this the surplus is simply dropped.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Game.Igi1.World.WeaponSoundPlayer
member.summary: Makes a gun sound, on the two-sample rule the weapon records are built around.

remarks.para: A weapon row carries two sound names, and which of them is used depends on a third field. Maximum Rounds/Burst of one or less means a single sample per shot — a pistol, a rifle, the shotgun. Above one and the gun starts its fire sound as a loop when it opens up and stops the loop with a separate loop-end sample when it stops, which is what the second name is for and why an automatic's fire sound in the data is named ak47_loop rather than ak47_1.
Playing an automatic as one sample per round instead would be both wrong and worse: the round rate is faster than the sample is long, so the shots would overlap into mush and burn a voice each.

member.name: M:OpenIGI.Game.Igi1.World.WeaponSoundPlayer.Parameters(System.String,System.Boolean)
member.summary: The voice a shot is played on.

remarks.para: The player's own weapon is NOT positional, and making it so was wrong. The gun is held in the player's own hands: its position relative to the head does not change, however much the camera turns. Placing it in the world and letting the listener rotate around it made the shot slide across the stereo image as the mouse moved, which is exactly the thing that cannot happen in reality — the camera moved, the gun did not.

It is also what the original does, though by accident rather than intent: it plays the shot at the player's own position, and its pan is the lateral offset from the listener, which for a source sitting on the listener is zero. A flat centred voice reaches the same place directly.

member.name: T:OpenIGI.Game.Igi1.World.WorldCell
member.summary: The broad-phase cell an object occupies — the loose-octree level its bounding box fits into.

remarks.para: From 0x4C67E0, which the position commit (0x4C6940) calls with an object's world AABB. A box fits in a cell of size 2^k exactly when its two corners agree in every bit above k, so the cell size is the highest bit at which the corners differ — one bsr over the OR of the three per-axis XORs, and no comparisons at all.

is 0x40000000, which is the same ±2^30 world cube the terrain octree spans — the collision index and the terrain share their bounds. is 8192 units, i.e. two metres, the finest the broad phase ever goes.

member.name: F:OpenIGI.Game.Igi1.World.WorldCell.MaximumSize
member.summary: The largest cell — the half-extent of the world cube the terrain octree also uses.
